articles.title: PNP reminds gamers not to imitate crimes in real life amid GTA 6 release
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Friday reminded video game enthusiasts not to imitate criminal activities and violence depicted in video games following the release of Grand Theft Auto VI…

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 10:18am
The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Friday reminded video game enthusiasts not to imitate criminal activities and violence depicted in video games amid the release of a "highly anticipated" game.
In a statement, PNP chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. pointed out the importance of distinguishing between digital entertainment and real-world conduct.

“Entertainment must never blur our understanding of right and wrong. What may be permissible in a virtual world has no place in real life when it violates the law, endangers others, or disregards human life,” Nartatez said.

While the PNP did not identify any specific game, the statement comes amid the release of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) which prompted police departments in the United States, United Kingdom, and Australia to remind players against imitating criminal activities depicted in virtual settings.
After 13 years of anticipation and an estimated production cost of at least $1 billion, the highly anticipated video game GTA 6 has finally been released, Reuters reported on Thursday.
The latest installment in the blockbuster video game franchise became available in New Zealand at midnight on Thursday, with its global rollout following different time zones.
Since its debut in 1997, GTA has grown into one of the best-selling video game series of all time, building a massive global following over nearly three decades, according to the report.
The PNP chief, meanwhile, reminded the public that acts of violence has "real world consequences."

“Every act of violence in the real world has consequences that cannot be reversed by a reset button or a respawn. We must strengthen awareness among our youth that firearms are not toys, violence is never a solution, and protecting human life must always come first,” he said.
Nartatez urged young Filipinos to exercise sound judgment both online and offline when exposed to content depicting violence and unlawful behavior.

“Enjoy your games but never allow fiction to dictate your actions in reality. Be responsible digital citizens, respect the rule of law, and remember that real-life choices carry real-life consequences,” he said. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: 'Crypto King' faked kidnapping, created video for sympathy, defence says
articles.summary: A lawyer defending one of so-called "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski’s alleged kidnappers says the kidnapping was a "farce" and that Pleterski created a video pretending to be kidnapped in order to gain…

blocks.text: Toronto·New

A lawyer defending one of so-called "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski’s alleged kidnappers says the kidnapping was a "farce" and that Pleterski created a video pretending to be kidnapped in order to gain sympathy from his investors, who were trying to recover funds from him.
Lawyer for alleged kidnapper says Aiden Pleterski faked video so his investors would see it, have sympathy
'Crypto King' faked kidnapping, defence says

A lawyer defending one of so-called "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski's alleged kidnappers says the kidnapping was a "farce" and that Pleterski created a video pretending to be kidnapped in order to gain sympathy from his investors.
Pleterski denied both assertions while being cross-examined Thursday during the Toronto trial for three of his alleged kidnappers in Ontario Superior Court.

The video, which was played for the jury earlier in the trial and was previously obtained by CBC News, shows a beaten Pleterski apologizing to his investors and explaining what happened to their money.
Defence lawyer Leora Shemesh suggested Pleterski made the video himself to go viral and be seen by his investors, who were trying to recover their lost funds through a bankruptcy proceeding.
"This is an apology that's going to your very angry investors, who were going to see you with two black eyes and take pity and sympathy with you," she said.

items: Secretly recorded videos of 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski meeting alleged kidnapper played at trial
'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski testifies he was beaten, tortured during alleged kidnapping

blocks.text: Shemesh is representing Alfredo Paladino who is charged — alongside Akil Heywood and Rakeem Henry — with kidnapping and extorting Pleterski.
Pleterski previously testified that he was beaten, tortured and thought he was going to die during the three-day ordeal in early December 2022.

From left, Alfredo Paladino, Akil Heywood and Rakeem Henry are accused of kidnapping and extorting the so-called 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski in December 2022. (Evan Mitsui/CBC, atlanticmastoronto/Instagram)

The Crown is alleging Heywood was the "driving force" behind the kidnapping and lost money investing with Pleterski, while Paladino and Henry carried out the kidnapping. Paladino and Henry are also charged with firearm and assault offences. All three men have pleaded not guilty.

Pleterski, who turned 28 on Wednesday, was convicted of fraud last month in connection with more than $30 million he took from investors to trade on their behalf. Instead, he spent much of it on his lifestyle. He has yet to be sentenced.
Pleterski questioned about kidnapping video
Pleterski testified Thursday that his kidnappers recorded the video while he was being held in a basement and instructed him on what to say.
"They told me to take all the blame for absolutely everything," he said.

Shemesh went through the transcript of the video line-by-line and questioned Pleterski about why he was including specific personal details such as how he was charged with assaulting his girlfriend in Florida and the year he began investing with his own money.
"During a kidnapping you told them that?" Shemesh pointedly asked him.
Pleterski said he was instructed to explain his story from the beginning and a lot of information, including the incident involving his girlfriend, was public at the time.
Defence lawyer Leora Shemesh, seen at right in this courtroom sketch, is representing Alfredo Paladino, right, in the trial involving the alleged kidnapping of Pleterski. (Pam Davies/CBC)

He testified that some of what he said in the nearly 14-minute video was true, some information was false — he said he was forced to say it by his kidnappers — and some he just said himself without instruction.

In the video, Pleterski details assets he "dispersed" to his former landlord Sandeep Gupta before his bankruptcy proceeding began, including luxury vehicles and at least two Rolex watches and a Jacob & Co. watch that he testified he bought for more than $300,000.

items: Crypto King's alleged kidnappers’ trial hears call Aiden Pleterski made to landlord asking for $3M
'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski testifies about escape attempt during alleged kidnapping

blocks.text: Pleterski testified Gupta wasn't actually hiding assets. He said he only told the kidnappers that so he could be released to set up a meeting with Gupta in hopes he would realize Pleterski was in trouble and alert the police.
Pleterski testified that he sold the Jacob & Co. watch and said he believed he got cash for it, but didn't remember who he sold it to or when, nor how he received the cash.
"Sandeep Gupta had your cars, Sandeep Gupta had your jewelry and Sandeep Gupta was holding money for you," Shemesh said.
Gupta testified earlier in the trial and denied hiding any assets for Pleterski.
Pleterski partied at rapper Drake's home

Heywood's defence lawyer, Hussein Aly, finished his cross-examination of Pleterski Thursday afternoon after two days of continually accusing Pleterski of lying, both while running a fraudulent investment scheme and during his testimony in the kidnapping trial.

Pleterski testified that Heywood invested with him then began threatening him about getting his money back. Pleterski said he was afraid after receiving threats from many people, including Heywood, so he hired security.
Aly questioned Pleterski about why he would hire a security company that belonged to Heywood's friend if Pleterski was being threatened by Heywood.

Akil Heywood's lawyer Hussein Aly showed the jury this photo of a group including Akil Heywood wearing a hat standing next to rapper Drake and the security guard wearing a blue shirt. Champagnepapi is Drake's instagram handle. (Akil Heywood/Facebook)
The jury heard the company is owned by Drake's security guard and Aly showed them photos of Heywood, Drake and the security guard together.
"You saw these photos on Akil Heywood's Instagram," Aly said to Pleterski.
Pleterski responded that he doesn't remember seeing them.
Aly also questioned why Pleterski went to a party at Drake's house in the spring of 2022 if he knew that Heywood was friends with the rapper.

Pleterski said he didn't know Heywood was going to be there, but said Heywood asked him for his money while at Drake's house, and that the security guard noticed the conversation, approached them, then put his hand on Heywood's shoulder and said "not here."

items: 'Crypto King' or 'Lying King'? Aiden Pleterski says he was neither at alleged kidnappers' trial

blocks.text: Aly has suggested Pleterski made up Heywood's involvement in the alleged kidnapping because he was mad about Heywood and another investor forcing Pleterski into bankruptcy.
"I could ask you questions for 100 days," Aly said to Pleterski. "You're never going to admit that you're lying about Akil Heywood's involvement in what happened to you."
Cross examination of Pleterski is expected to continue tomorrow afternoon.

articles.summary: The results are in – Samsung unveils the finalists of Solve for Tomorrow 2026 in the Philippines, the annual student competition under its global program, putting the spotlight on young Filipino…

blocks.text: The results are in – Samsung unveils the finalists of Solve for Tomorrow 2026 in the Philippines, the annual student competition under its global program, putting the spotlight on young Filipino changemakers ready to make a difference.
The top 10 teams that will move forward in the competition are:

items: Team SAGIP from Quezon City Science High School;
Team CheckMite from Siaton Science High School;
Ligtas Skwela from Philippine Science High School Caraga Region Campus;
Team HydroHero from Valenzuela City School of Mathematics and Science;
From Pulp to Brine from Lanao Del Norte Provincial Science and Technology;
Team KINAIYAHAN from Bayawan City Science and Technology Education Center High School;
Team KUHOL-LECTOR from Philippine Science High School Main;
Team AgriSpectra from Eastern Visayas Regional Science High School;
Team VoltROOT from Tagbilaran City Science High School; and
Team CanalCare from Baguio City National Science High School.

blocks.text: As part of Samsung’s global commitment to youth tech education, Solve for Tomorrow provides students with a platform to turn their ideas into real-world solutions in partnership with the Department of Education. The initiative encourages students in Grades 8 to 10 from government-managed science high schools nationwide to develop innovative, STEM-driven solutions that address challenges in their own communities. Top 10 finalists will vie to be among the three grand winners, who will receive almost PHP 2 million in total of cash prizes and Samsung devices for their schools, teams, and teacher advisers.

For 2026, Samsung received over 500 submissions, involving more than 1000 students from all 15 regions in the country. Each team, composed of up to four student members, was challenged to develop a proposal inspired by one of three themes: Environmental Sustainability through Technology, Social Change through Tech and Sport, and Solving Community Problems with Artificial Intelligence (AI).

Samsung also brought together a distinguished panel of industry leaders from the fields of technology, innovation, and education to serve as judges – Alwyn Rosel, Executive Director of QBO Innovation; Ria Liza Canlas, President of the Filipino Women Inventors Society; Jaton Zulueta, Executive Director and Founder of AHA Learning Center; Grahssel Dungca, Luzon Programs Co-Lead of DEVCON Philippines; and Jun Guevara, Head of Corporate Marketing at Samsung Electronics Philippines.
The 10 finalists will also be mentored by Samsung experts to refine proposals and build proof-of-concepts ahead of the final presentation.

blocks.text: White House national ⁠cyber director Sean ⁠Cairncross ​was ousted from his job, a person close to the White House told Reuters on Thursday, ⁠days after tech outages hit US air travel, banking and national security systems.

Cairncross oversaw cybersecurity policy and ⁠strategy across the federal government. Department of Defense chief information officer ​Kirsten Davies will ‌assume the position ‌temporarily, according to the source.
“The president fully supported firing Sean ‌Cairncross from his position,” said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Cairncross declined to comment on his departure.

Axios first reported Cairncross’s departure from the White House, citing anonymous officials claiming White House chief of staff Stephen Miller pushed for the personnel change because Cairncross “lacked the strong cyber credentials to perform the job”.

Technology-related outages have hit regularly over the last week, including a nationwide halt to air travel, a Microsoft outage that ‌hit email services and a temporary disruption to the US National Security Agency’s network.

The Trump administration ​has faced criticism over its response to the outages. The top US intelligence official said on Wednesday the disruptions to critical systems over the past week were separate service ⁠outages associated with maintenance and technical changes and not a ​coordinated or ​state-sponsored attack.

Cairncross was an ​executive at the Republican National Committee before assuming ​the cyber director ‌role. His ​successor will need ​to be confirmed by the Senate, which will be controlled by Democrats beginning in January.

articles.title: NAPOLCOM probes 6 cops in alleged P1.2M Caloocan robbery
articles.summary: The National Police Commission (NAPOLCOM) has launched an investigation against six police officers who are implicated in a robbery incident involving P1.2 million worth of valuables in Caloocan City.

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 9:13am

The National Police Commission (NAPOLCOM) has launched an investigation against six police officers who are implicated in a robbery incident involving P1.2 million worth of valuables in Caloocan City.

A complainant filed a complaint before the NAPOLCOM office on Thursday against six police officers, including the alleged mastermind, Police Major Jasper Benedict Santos, according to a report by GMA News’ Chino Gaston on Unang Balita.

NAPOLCOM said that according to the complainant, Santos of the Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (CIDG) contacted him after learning that the complainant was selling a gold bracelet worth P700,000.
They agreed to meet on November 16 at a restaurant in Caloocan City, where Santos allegedly sent his driver and another companion to inspect the jewelry.
The complainant, who was accompanied by a police officer friend, was later instructed to proceed to another area to meet another supposed buyer.
Upon arriving, several armed men allegedly forced the two victims to lie face down on the road before taking them into a vehicle.

The complainant claimed the suspects staged an arrest by including another individual whom they supposedly had been monitoring and had just apprehended. He became suspicious when the individual was not handcuffed and appeared familiar with the armed men.
The complainant alleged that Santos was inside the vehicle, holding a firearm and pointing it at him.

He identified a police corporal as the driver and a former patrolman as another occupant. The ex-cop allegedly pointed a firearm at his face, while another unidentified man threatened him with a knife. The police corporal also allegedly threatened to kill him if he looked at the suspects.
The suspects reportedly took his gold bracelet, cellphone and firearm.

The complainant said the suspects later claimed that some of their belongings had been left on a motorcycle near a subdivision between Malabon and Valenzuela. However, they could no longer locate the bracelet, while the motorcycle was also missing.
NAPOLCOM said that the Philippine National Police (PNP) investigation also identified a police captain, a police senior master sergeant, and a patrolman as among those implicated in the incident.
Two unidentified individuals were also involved.
Santos, who was presented during the press briefing, denied the accusations and said he would explain his side before the court.

The complainant also disclosed that Santos's sibling had offered to replace his missing jewelry and other belongings, along with additional compensation, in exchange for dropping the complaint. He rejected the offer.
He also raised concerns about possible intimidation as unidentified individuals had been seen circling his residence.
Meanwhile, NAPOLCOM Commissioner Rafael Vicente Calinisan said the commission's investigation remains ongoing and would cover all individuals implicated.
Calinisan urged the remaining police personnel implicated in the incident to surrender voluntarily.
"Sa mga kasama ni Major Santos na hinahanap pa, sumuko na kayo. Hinahanap na kayo ng mga pulis. Huwag na ninyong pahirapan ang ating mga kapwa pulis na hulihin at arestuhin kayo," he said.

He called for stricter recruitment procedures, comprehensive background investigations and properly administered neuropsychological examinations to prevent individuals with questionable backgrounds from entering the police service.

"We have to remove the inept, corrupt, and undisciplined cops from the organization and ensure that those who will be recruited moving forward are qualified and committed to serving the public," Calinisan said. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: [Vantage Point] The ASEAN Summit’s billions: Who pays, who gains?
articles.summary: When a government claims an investment victory, it should explain how the country will profit, rather than letting people confuse an American sales receipt with Filipino wealth

blocks.text: Washington’s US$17-billion headline sounds like a massive windfall, yet most of that money comes from pre-existing airplane orders and proposed loans rather than fresh foreign investment. Before celebrating, Filipinos deserve a clear breakdown of what we are actually buying, what we owe, and what stays in our economy now that the summit has ended.
Washington has put a big price tag on President Donald Trump’s Manila visit: over US$17 billion in business deals and strategic investments for American companies.

Before celebrating that number as a Philippine win, we should ask: Who is buying, who is selling, and who eventually pays? When a Philippine company buys from America, it can support US jobs and benefit Filipino travelers. However, buying a product is not the same as foreign money flowing into our economy to build businesses.

President Trump has one priority on his mind: the American people.$17 billion in commercial deals and strategic investments for U.S. companies secured. 🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/pkGCaZJX9z— The White House (@WhiteHouse) November 18, 2026

The White House’s November 18 fact sheet covers commercial deals and investment announcements across the region. For our country, it lists an aircraft and engine sale valued by the White House at $12 billion, plus a proposed military loan exceeding $2 billion.
These two items work differently. Adding them together makes a flashy headline, but tells us little about the real income, business growth, or government debt those deals will create locally.

Look at the airplanes first. Philippine Airlines (PAL) said its agreements with Boeing and GE Aerospace were finalized on November 10, days before ASEAN leaders gathered in Manila for the ASEAN Summit.

PAL’s November 15 announcement traced these plans back to the Farnborough International Airshow in July. Boeing confirmed a finalized order for 15 Dreamliners, with the opportunity to buy five more. Simply put, this deal was underway before Trump’s plane landed.

This timeline does not make the order less real. Turning an early plan into a signed contract is a big step, and leaders love showcasing deals during visits. Still, to know what the summit achieved, we must separate existing deals from new ones created at the meeting. Otherwise, the same deal can be recycled and celebrated as a “new” win whenever a foreign leader visits.

We must also examine the plane count. PAL placed a firm order for 15 planes and has the opportunity to buy five more. Investors need to know when deposits and later payments fall due, how PAL will finance them, and when it can decide whether to buy the additional aircraft. A big headline answers none of these questions.

The $12-billion price tag raises questions. Company announcements do not mention that price, explain how much goes to planes versus engines, or show whether the optional planes are included. Thus, we cannot tell from Washington’s headline how much PAL will pay. Nor should we guess by assuming undisclosed discounts. The honest approach is sticking to what companies shared and leaving unknowns open.

Buying new airplanes gives an airline great tools, but the sticker price does not equal money earned by the Philippines. The benefits at home depend on how PAL uses those planes, how many passengers and how much cargo they carry, what jobs they support, and what remains after operating and financing costs.
When a government claims an investment victory, it should explain how the country will profit, rather than letting people confuse an American sales receipt with Filipino wealth.

PAL has a good reason to upgrade. Newer planes can burn less fuel, replace aging jets, and carry more passengers and cargo. Those upgrades can benefit our country even though the planes are built abroad.
But are the revenues these planes generate over their lifetimes cover acquisition, financing, and operating costs? Or did they just make a political summit look good?

PAL’s November 4 results release shows why we must watch those numbers. In the first nine months of 2026, PAL brought in $2.50 billion in revenue, up 4%. However, it posted a $159-million net loss mainly because fuel costs rose by $339.4 million.

PAL generated $247 million in free cash flow during the period and ended September with $879 million in cash and short-term investments, including net proceeds from $350 million in five-year senior unsecured notes.

These numbers show that cash on hand, accounting earnings, and borrowed money are separate things. Investors must weigh future airplane bills against operating cash flow, existing debt payments, and delivery dates.

Fuel savings can improve operating margins, while financing adds to the cost of owning the aircraft. PAL says deliveries are scheduled in the next decade, so investors should assess costs and benefits as they fall due.

Government borrowing needs its own careful look. The White House said both countries would pursue a Foreign Military Financing loan package exceeding $2 billion. Its announcement gave no final loan terms or disbursement details. Any borrowing under the package would carry repayment obligations, with the cost to taxpayers depending on the final terms.

Naturally, a strong military has value beyond profit. Protecting our seas, bridges, and borders keeps the country safe so businesses can grow and people can work. Still, the public deserves basic details before judging affordability: Who borrows the money, what is the interest rate, how many years do we pay it back, and what will maintaining new gear cost? Because defense is vital, we need smart financing so our military can run and repair equipment long after publicity photo opportunities end.
Manila should publish a public register identifying signed contracts, optional purchases, proposed loans, and early promises. It should note earlier announcements and track progress.

Every project should show local spending, Filipino jobs created, debts taken on, and expected benefits. Washington rightly measures success by American sales and jobs. Our government must show what Filipinos gain, what we owe, and whether benefits last after visiting leaders fly home. – Rappler.com

articles.title: More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged
articles.summary: African countries at the UN climate summit in Turkey are demanding more funding from developed nations to help them cope with climate change.

blocks.text: In Uganda's northern Karamoja region, Elijah Lobur and his family now eat just one meal a day.
A severe drought that began in April has destroyed crops, while food brought in from elsewhere has become increasingly unaffordable.
"Seven months without rain has brought us to this point where we now live in hunger," the 44-year-old farmer, who lives with his grandmother, wife and five children, told the BBC.
"Even some of the wild plants that we used to eat have withered and dried up."
Local officials say more than 90% of crops have failed in the region, where agriculture is largely rain-fed.
Further south, in Malawi, Mathews Nkhambala has experienced the devastating effects of flooding.
In April 2024, barely a year after Tropical Cyclone Freddy devastated the country's southern region, floods displaced people in Chikwawa district.
Nkhambala fled to higher ground with his wife and four children as floodwaters swept through his village.
"As we reached a safe height, we saw our house swept away right in front of our eyes. Everything I had was gone," he told the BBC.
He lost a harvest of 15 bags of sorghum and part of his farmland. His children were so traumatised that they stopped going to school.
"They refused to go to school for many months. They were so disturbed," he recalled.
After relocating and trying to rebuild his life, Nkhambala is now facing another climate challenge - this time a lack of rain.
"This time we fear there may be no harvest. I have no clue what I will do."
A government assessment after Cyclone Freddy found that Malawi had experienced more than 50 disasters linked to storms, floods, landslides and droughts since 1980, affecting millions of people.

While Uganda and Malawi are suffering the effects of climate change and their governments are asking for assistance adapting to the new global weather patterns, they are among 23 African countries yet to submit National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) to the UN climate convention secretariat.

These are the plans that detail how climate change has affected them and the risks they face, and so help make a case for what assistance they need. Without them, experts say, it becomes difficult to secure funding.

"Our region has experienced cyclical droughts for decades, but there has been no action plan to tackle these climate impacts," said Milton Lorpia, who works for Warrior Squad Foundation in Karamoja region of Uganda.
"If only such a plan were in place and implemented, it would certainly have helped us."

The African Group of Negotiators at the ongoing UN climate summit (COP31) in Turkey is pushing for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035, from an annual $40bn (£30bn) baseline that it says developed countries committed to providing by 2025. The interpretation of that commitment remains contested.
The proposal was not accepted for formal negotiations at the summit, although African negotiators have continued to push for it.
The funding is intended to help vulnerable countries prepare for and withstand climate change-induced extreme weather, such as droughts, floods and wildfires.
But the European Union, one of the largest providers of climate finance, says the priority should be ensuring existing commitments reach vulnerable countries rather than setting new funding targets.

"We haven't come to the table with additional monies or additional capital. It's about what we have committed already and ensuring it's deployed," Darragh O'Brien, who leads the EU delegation at COP31 on behalf of the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, told a press conference.
He acknowledged that developing countries faced difficulties accessing available funding, saying the process needed to be improved.
Wopke Hoekstra, the European Commission's climate commissioner, also argued that the summit should focus on delivering existing pledges rather than making new ones.

"If you are a vulnerable nation in the Pacific or one of the LDCs (Least Developed Countries) and the money is in the bank but does not land on the ground then it is effectively meaningless," he said.
Hoekstra said the EU had provided $30bn of the $100bn in climate finance committed by developed countries in recent years, adding that other wealthy nations should contribute more.

The scale of the need is substantial. According to the UN's Adaptation Gap Report published last year, sub-Saharan Africa requires about $51bn annually in adaptation finance, while the Middle East and North Africa needs $112bn.
Globally, developing countries will need about $300bn annually by 2035, according to the UN's latest report. Yet they received only about 10% of that amount from developed countries in 2024.
Climate-related loss and damage in Africa is projected to cost $440bn between 2020 and 2030, according to Nairobi-based think tank Power Shift Africa.
Under the 2015 Paris climate agreement, developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations, including for climate adaptation.
But why have so many African countries failed to prepare plans that could help them identify their needs and build resilience?

"If you look closely, the countries that are yet to submit their NAPs are already dealing with multiple crises, including debt distress, economic pressures and other issues," said David Abudho, climate justice lead at the aid agency, Oxfam.
"Their governments' ability to invest in climate adaptation is limited."
Sheila Apiny, regional climate justice adviser at ActionAid, said the lack of plans reflected a wider shortage of financial and technical support.
"The absence of NAPs in so many countries is, in itself, evidence of an adaptation finance and capacity gap," she argued.
She said this created a vicious cycle - countries lack support to prepare their plans, while not having the plans makes it harder to secure funding for climate resilience.

"When countries lack adequate adaptation planning and, more importantly, the resources to implement those plans, governments are forced into a cycle of responding to disasters instead of preventing or reducing their impacts," said Amos Wemanya, senior climate adviser at Power Shift Africa.

"Instead of investing in early warning systems, climate-resilient agriculture, water security and flood protection, scarce public resources are repeatedly diverted towards emergency relief and reconstruction. This costs more over time and leaves communities increasingly vulnerable."
African negotiators acknowledge that adaptation plans help countries prioritise investments and attract funding, but argue that their absence should not be used to deny them financial support.

"Of course, having a comprehensive NAP helps countries prioritise investments and prepare proposals for climate finance," said Mahlet Eyassu Melkie, a senior strategic adviser to Ethiopia's COP32 presidency.

"But Africa's adaptation financing needs are based on scientific assessments, climate vulnerability, national priorities and regional estimates – not simply on whether every country has submitted a particular planning document."
The UN Development Programme, which has helped more than 45 countries prepare their plans, said NAPs can help governments mobilise international support and coordinate climate action.
Fred Njehu, a Pan-African political strategist at Greenpeace Africa, said their absence could nevertheless create significant obstacles.

"It is fair to acknowledge that missing adaptation plans act as a major functional barrier that severely bottlenecks the speed, volume and quality of international funding a country can access," he said.
But having a plan does not guarantee the money needed to implement it.
"Even countries that have completed their NAPs have not received money anywhere near what they require for implementation of their adaptation plans," Apiny said.
Kenya offers an example of how adaptation measures can help communities cope with climate pressures.

In the country's arid and semi-arid south-east, concrete sand dams slow the flow of seasonal rivers, allowing sand to accumulate and store water underground. Communities can access it during dry periods using hand pumps or by scooping it out.

UK charity Sand Dams Worldwide and its local partner, the Africa Sand Dam Foundation, said they had built about 1,300 such dams, improving access to water as droughts become more frequent and intense.
But many vulnerable communities elsewhere on the continent are still waiting for similar interventions.
Back in drought-hit Karamoja, Lobur wonders how different things might have been if farmers had access to small-scale irrigation schemes.
"We do have some underground water sources in some places. If there were proper plans and programmes, we could have tapped them to grow food, but we are having to live in hunger instead," Lobur said.
"My grandmother keeps reminding us how she lost eight children during a famine-like situation in 1982, and we all fear we might perish like that too."

articles.title: CN derailments into Skeena River raise fresh concerns over shipping hazardous materials through northwest B.C.
articles.summary: The company says a suspected rockslide pushed a locomotive and several cars down an embankment and into the waters of the Skeena River Tuesday, with diesel from the locomotive then leaking more than…

image.caption: Drone footage shared with CBC News shows a CN Rail locomotive and several cars still in the Skeena River two days after a derailment near Terrace, B.C. The derailment has prompted questions over the safety of transporting hazardous materials through northwest B.C. (Carl J. Reibin)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New

The company says a suspected rockslide pushed a locomotive and several cars down an embankment and into the waters of the Skeena River Tuesday, with diesel from the locomotive then leaking more than a kilometre downstream. It's the second such incident this year, following a similar derailment during extreme weather this past March.
Company is cleaning up 2nd diesel spill into Skeena River this year following suspected rockslide

The debate over shipping hazardous materials by rail has been reignited after a CN Rail train came off the tracks in northwest B.C., leaking diesel into the salmon-bearing Skeena River for the second time in eight months.

The company says a suspected rockslide pushed a locomotive and several cars down an embankment and into the water Tuesday, with diesel from the locomotive then leaking more than a kilometre downstream.
It's the second such incident this year, following a similar derailment during extreme weather this past March.

In an update Thursday morning, CN Rail said it had repaired the track and traffic is running again, and the B.C. government says a containment boom and absorbent pads are in place and a surface water sampling plan has been drafted.
The province also says it's asked CN Rail to provide an estimate for how much diesel was spilled, but so far, the volume has not been shared.
Drone footage from the site shows a visible sheen traveling downstream.
Former NDP MP Taylor Bachrach, who lives in the region and previously served as the party's transport critic, called the derailments a "wake-up call."
"The railroad, for hundreds of kilometres in our region, goes right next to the Skeena River," he said, identifying it as highly important for salmon.
"When we're talking about the shipment of dangerous goods along that rail line, the implications, the consequences of a major disaster are really unthinkable."

The debate over rail shipments is especially fraught in northwest B.C., where the Port of Prince Rupert has emerged as key to shipping energy products to overseas Asian markets in light of the U.S.-Canada trade war.
What politicians get wrong about the B.C. oil tanker ban
Even so, efforts to build a pipeline to transport heavy crude oil to the North Coast have been resisted due to concerns about environmental impacts.
Likewise, proposals like that from Calgary-based Strathcona Resources to ship up to 250,000 barrels of Canadian oil to Prince Rupert a day have also met with opposition.
They are made more challenging by the Liberal government's support of the Oil Tanker Moratorium Act, which blocks large oil tankers from travelling along B.C.'s northern coast.
Concerns over response time
No major spill incidents were recorded between Terrace and Prince Rupert in the decade prior to this year, according to provincial data.
Even so, the more recent spills have First Nations in the area worried about the increased train traffic through the sensitive region.
CN Rail says cleanup efforts are underway after a train derailed into the Skeena River on Nov. 17, 2026. (Submitted by Carl J. Reibin)
Kitsumkalum First Nation Chief Councillor Troy Sam said he wants to make sure the province and industry groups work with First Nations to improve response times.
"My position is to make sure this doesn't happen again," he said. "What did we learn from this incident and how could we respond better?"

Gitxsan Hereditary Chief Skogam'Lahkx Toby Howard said his government is calling for all cargo train traffic between Burns Lake and Prince Rupert to be put on hold until the full track can be inspected for safety.
"The whole system ... it's pretty old," he said. "There are a lot of things we need to address."
Diesel leaking into Skeena River after train derails near Terrace, B.C.

Peter Ross, an environmental toxicologist with the Raincoast Conservation Foundation, said that while diesel tends to dissipate and evaporate on its own, it still poses a risk to fish and wildlife who come into contact with it.
And, he said, the two spills within a few months raise larger concerns.
"I think this really speaks to the dangers of transport when it comes to petrochemicals," he said.

items: 2 hospitalized after CN Rail train derails into Skeena River near Terrace, B.C.
Gitxsan hereditary chiefs call for halt to rail cargo as diesel leaks from train derailment along Skeena River

blocks.text: While he was confident officials would manage the spill, Ross wondered whether they would see the bigger picture.
"It's something we do very poorly as a society, is add all of these cumulative effects together to try to define the risk to fish and wildlife," he said.
With files from Catherine Garrett and Jason Peters

articles.title: [Rear View] ASEAN postscript: Marcos forgot who his real audience is
articles.summary: Marcos and Trump took center stage as two men in the early stages of lameduckery. Both carry deep trust deficits, and both have suffered major political reversals.

blocks.text: To be fair, chairing the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and hosting its summit is an obligation. But the Marcos administration couldn’t resist turning it into a vanity project.

Parts of Metro Manila plagued by squalor amid plenty were transformed, for three days, into a painted-over, water-hosed showcase of the true, the good, and the beautiful. Protest groups were asked to keep the summit a protest-free zone, as though airing grievances while guests were in town were a breach of manners.

When the protesters marched anyway, police met them with truncheons and shields. More than 300 were arrested across Metro Manila and nearby provinces, loaded into police vans and held at Camp Bagong Diwa until Air Force One had cleared the tarmac. The administration conveniently forgot that constitutional rights are not suspended when foreign guests arrive.
Was it worth it?
With his term nearing its close, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is eager to claim his spot on the global stage.

He has spoken all year of the region’s “defining moment,” but has had little to say about his own administration’s, confronted as it is by rising inflation, gas prices, unmitigated corruption, and the creeping breakdown of public services.

He wanted to make a good impression on the visiting heads of state, his regional peers, and the leaders of the major powers, above all US President Donald Trump. He forgot that such impressions are fleeting; these leaders have their own troubles at home. The lasting impression lies with the people, who saw in the hosting another example of an administration out of touch with daily realities.

Marcos grinned throughout his face-to-face meetings with Trump, even arranging a brief reunion between Trump and his mother, the former first lady, wheelchair-bound but still able to turn on the charm for a man she first met decades ago on the New York party circuit.
Posting on Truth Social as he left Manila, Trump praised Marcos as “a powerful leader, and a man of high integrity and substance.” It was the money shot Marcos had longed for.

blocks.caption: Trump announces ‘biggest trade deal’ between Philippines, US

blocks.text: Marcos and Trump took center stage as two men in the early stages of lameduckery. Both carry deep trust deficits, and both have suffered major political reversals. In the wake of his party’s resounding midterm defeat, Trump, true to form, has doubled down on his unpopular agenda. Faced with mounting economic woes, Marcos would rather focus on his political survival.

The global stage offers refuge and respite, however brief, a place where he can shine and be applauded by his peers. After the handshakes, the gala dinners, the gabfest, and the photo opportunities, the delegations flew home, perhaps impressed by the hospitality. But foreign leaders and their entourages will not vote in 2028.

The President wanted the world to watch him. For three days, Metro Manila became a stage set and a conflict zone. We got an extended holiday, but commuters were stranded by road closures, vendors were cleared from motorcade routes, and protesters were loaded into police vans for exercising a constitutional right their President swore to defend.
In trying to impress the world, the President forgot who his real audience is, and they were never inside the convention hall. – Rappler.com
Joey Salgado is a former journalist, and a government and political communications practitioner. He served as spokesperson for former vice president Jejomar Binay.

articles.title: PNP on ex-Sara Duterte staff members: No rescue, release happened because they were not 'held'
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Friday clarified that there was "no rescue or release" of a former household staff member of Vice President Sara Duterte and four other individuals.

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 8:44am
The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Friday clarified that there was "no rescue or release" of a former household staff member of Vice President Sara Duterte and four other individuals.
In a statement, the PNP pointed out that the concerned ex-former staff members of Duterte were not being held captive when police accompanied their lawyers to a hotel in Taguig City on November 17.
"There was no rescue and no release, because no one was being held," the PNP said.
Patay ang tatlong lalaki matapos mabagsakan ng tangke ng tubig sa Abulug, Cagayan.
Safe
On Wednesday, Duterte’s camp said that two of her former staff members who allegedly received threats to their lives were already safe and sound following a rescue operation with the help of police.

Duterte's spokesperson, Atty. Paolo Panelo, said the two former staff members were recruited by a private individual to work at a resort in Boracay in October. They were later brought to Manila under the pretext of training for their jobs.
Panelo claimed that their employer told them that the threats against them would be quelled if they signed affidavits containing allegations against the Vice President, which they refused to sign.
Duterte is currently facing an impeachment trial in the Senate.
Police assistance

According to the PNP, two legal counsels went to Fort Bonifacio Police Sub-Station 1 in Taguig on November 17 and requested police assistance in fetching a former Duterte staff member and four other individuals from a hotel in Bonifacio Global City.
Police personnel accompanied the lawyers and found the five individuals, who were not restrained and did not report any immediate threat to their safety.
All five came down from their hotel rooms on their own and went with the police officers to the station, the PNP said.

“At the station, the individuals declined to execute affidavits regarding their reported captivity and did not identify anyone allegedly involved or disclose the source of the supposed threats,” the PNP said.
“Their legal counsels instead executed and submitted an affidavit for documentation, which became the basis for the police blotter dated November 17, 2026,” it added.
After the documentation, the five individuals left the station without raising any further concern or requesting additional assistance, according to the PNP.
The PNP said it remains ready to receive complaints and sworn statements and provide appropriate police assistance and protection to anyone reporting threats.
But it also reiterated its commitment to remain apolitical and carry out its mandate fairly and impartially, regardless of political affiliations or differences. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Religious messages agriculture secretary emailed to staff deemed unconstitutional
articles.summary:
A federal judge ruled that messages sent by Brooke Rollins to USDA workers suggest Christianity is a shared faith and violate the first amendment

Religious messages that US agriculture…

blocks.text: Religious messages that US agriculture secretary Brooke Rollins emailed to the agency’s 100,000 employees were unconstitutional, and she must be careful to avoid proselytizing when communicating with workers, a federal judge ruled Thursday.

Rollins sent the messages, which included Christian messages and images, from her official email account on holidays such as Independence Day, Thanksgiving, Christmas and Easter. She did not send messages commemorating holidays from other religions.

“And so, like the very first disciples to encounter our risen Lord in the Upper Room almost two thousand years ago, this Easter let us too be alive with hope, full of Paschal joy, and confident in the mission each of us has been called for,” Rollins wrote in a 5 April email, marking Easter.

US district judge Trina Thompson in San Francisco said the emails violated the first amendment’s establishment clause, pointing to her position of authority, her use of an official email account and the messages suggesting that Christianity is the shared faith of Department of Agriculture (USDA) workers.
The USDA did not respond to a request for comment.

Employees cannot realistically opt out of reading emails from their agency director, and the messages could coerce them to hide their own faith or feel pressure to adopt Rollins’ Christian faith, Thompson ruled.

When disseminating religious messages, Rollins must stop if a colleague asks her to. “Cannot create a hostile work environment through persistent unwelcome advances” and “cannot use official authority to pressure subordinates” are commands that were quoted directly from a USDA policy on workplace religious expression that Rollins herself adopted.

Rollins may discuss her faith with interested colleagues, share why her faith is meaningful to her, politely invite co-workers to religious events and express her views in appropriate conversations, Thompson ruled, again quoting directly from Rollins’ policy.
Six USDA employees and the National Federation of Federal Employees, a labor union representing 19,000 USDA workers, brought the suit in May.

Former Commission on Audit chairperson Gamaliel Cordoba.
Commission on Audit website
MANILA, Philippines — Former Commission on Audit chairperson Gamaliel Cordoba has taken his oath as an Associate Justice of the Supreme Court.
Cordoba took his oath before Chief Justice Rodil Zalameda on Thursday, November 19.
He replaces Associate Justice Amy Lazaro-Javier, who reached compulsory retirement on November 16.
Before his appointment to the high court, he served as COA Chairperson from 2022to 2026.

Before that, he held several key positions in the Office of the President, which include appointments secretary with the rank of undersecretary from 2006 to 2007, undersecretary from 2003 to 2006, assistant executive secretary from 2002 to 2003, and technical assistant with the rank of Director IV from 2001 to 2002.
He also served as director of the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corp. from 2008 to 2009.
Cordoba is the third justice of the Supreme Court to be appointed by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

articles.title: [Market Rider] Will NGCP’s Project Airbag help solve Philippines’ high power cost?
articles.summary: Filipino consumers will ultimately bear the financial risk and cost of building energy storage under NGCP's Project Airbag

items: The National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) faces opposition from industry groups regarding its Project Airbag, a P700-billion initiative aimed at deploying 10,000 MW of battery energy storage systems to stabilize the power grid.

Critics, including the Philippine Independent Power Producers Association (PIPPA) and Philippine Solar and Storage Energy Alliance (PSSEA), argue that NGCP's ownership of storage assets creates conflicts of interest and undermines market competition, as it could lead to unfair advantages over private generation companies.

Both PIPPA and PSSEA advocate for competitive procurement of storage services from private developers instead of allowing NGCP to rate-base its storage facilities, emphasizing the need to adhere to the Electric Power Industry Reform Act (EPIRA) to protect consumers from increased costs.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

The National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) again drew a strong pushback from its recent controversial program. This time, from industry peers, particularly the Philippine Independent Power Producers Association (PIPPA) and Philippine Solar and Storage Energy Alliance (PSSEA) in connection with its recently unveiled transmission-side energy storage project initiative called Project Airbag.

Project Airbag is yet one of those ambitious programs of NGCP that is seen off tangent from its structural role, with its planned P700-billion, five-year plan to deploy 10,000 megawatts (MW) of battery energy storage systems (BESS) purportedly to store excess electricity and release it during sudden shortages, peak demand, and grid disturbances.

blocks.caption: [Market Rider] Will NGCP’s Project Airbag help solve Philippines’ high power cost?

blocks.text: NGCP describes the project as a fast-response buffer or “shock absorber” (as it technically calls it) and a forward-thinking concept to stabilize the Philippine power grid, capitalizing on the generation constraints anticipated for the El Niño dry season phenomenon in 2027.

blocks.caption: Source: NGCP’s Project Airbag Media Briefer

blocks.text: As reported last November 9, NGCP will start Project Airbag shortly with a P59.5-billion, 850 MW Phase 1 rollout.

blocks.caption: Source: NGCP’s Project Airbag Media Briefer

blocks.text: Project Airbag is now under review by the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC). While purely framed by NGCP as a vital safety net against grid instability and a precautionary move for the 2027 El Niño, the project according to the PIPPA and PSSEA — sans its polite rhetoric — is but a plain and simple Trojan horse strategy of NGCP that raises major regulatory and economic questions, particularly on whether a transmission monopoly like it is should own, operate, and rate-base commercial-style storage assets.

PIPPA agrees with the urgent claim of NGCP to stabilize the power grid in preparation for the expected El Niño phenomenon in 2027. Nevertheless, it argues that NGCP should focus on delayed transmission reinforcements rather than entering the competitive storage sector. PIPPA asserts that storing and discharging electricity during supply shortages, grid disturbances, and evening peaks is inherently a generation function.

Under the Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001 (EPIRA) and NGCP’s franchise (Republic Act 9511), the power industry legally separates competitive generation from regulated transmission, prohibiting cross-ownership to prevent market distortion. Allowing NGCP to own and dispatch its own storage fleet while simultaneously acting as the system operator creates a severe conflict of interest, granting NGCP unfair dispatch control and information advantages over private generation companies (GenCos).

PIPPA further points out that rate-based NGCP storage creates an uneven playing field and shifts financial risks onto electricity consumers. Private BESS developers bear construction, technology, and utilization risks, recovering costs only through competitive wholesale markets or ERC-approved contracts, a challenge worsened by the ERC’s October 2026 suspension of the “reserve market” (the specialized sub-market within the Wholesale Electricity Spot Market or WESM) where NGCP is allowed to procure standby power capacities and ancillary services.

Conversely, if NGCP includes Project Airbag in its regulatory asset base, it is guaranteed a regulated return paid directly by consumers through transmission wheeling rates, regardless of asset utilization or cost-efficiency.

International benchmarks from the European Union and the United States reinforce that transmission operators should generally be barred from owning storage, with rare exceptions strictly ring-fenced from market participation.

To address grid reliability without undermining EPIRA, PIPPA urges the Department of Energy (DOE) and the ERC to reject rate-based BESS ownership by NGCP. Instead, PIPPA advocates the following actions:

items: NGCP should be required to competitively procure storage services from private third parties and transfer ongoing Project Airbag sites to qualified developers
ERC to expedite approvals for ancillary services procurement agreements (ASPAs) and enforce strict timelines for NGCP to finish pending system impact studies and grid connections
lift the “reserve market” suspension and launch competitive BESS auctions to attract private investment.

blocks.text: For the PSSEA, while it also supports the engineering value of grid-forming storage for frequency response, voltage support, and renewable energy integration, it warns that allowing NGCP to own and operate BESS without strict guardrails threatens fair market competition and risks burdening consumers with unnecessary fixed costs.

PSSEA emphasizes that NGCP already holds five powerful monopoly and regulatory roles, namely as sole transmission network provider, system operator (SO) exercising central dispatch, determiner of ancillary services (AS) requirements, sole AS buyer, and AS compliance monitor.
Under DOE Circular No. DC2023-04-0008, allowing NGCP to own BESS adds a sixth conflicting role — that of being a market seller.

Although Section 5.6 restricts SO-owned storage to “last resort” AS deployment, Section 5.5 permits transmission congestion management and upgrade deferment without clear dispatch limits. Because a single battery performs both functions simultaneously, NGCP could bypass private AS providers, leverage privileged grid information, and audit its own competitors while acting as both referee and player.

Furthermore, including storage in NGCP’s Regulatory Asset Base (RAB) forces consumers to pay guaranteed returns regardless of dispatch, creating risks of “double recovery” if the assets also earn market revenues.

International benchmarks from the US, Australia, India, and Germany show that system operators are structurally separated from asset ownership, and network-owned storage is strictly barred from commercial market trading.
To protect market integrity, PSSEA recommends limiting NGCP-owned BESS strictly to a Storage-as-a-Transmission-Only-Asset (SATOA) model under four core conditions:

items: confine dispatch strictly to reactive voltage support or last-resort congestion management and upgrade deferment when no private AS capacity is available, barring energy arbitrage and AS market participation
require a transparent, failed third-party tender before approving any NGCP-owned storage
restrict cost recovery exclusively to the RAB, crediting any incidental revenues back to consumers
mandate public logging and annual Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC)-appointed audits of every dispatch.

blocks.text: Alternatively, PSSEA proposes that NGCP identify optimal BESS locations and capacities, allowing the DOE to auction these projects to private Generation Companies.

blocks.caption: Source: NGCP’s Project Airbag Media Briefer

blocks.text: Under the EPIRA, the Philippine power sector is unbundled: generation and supply are competitive, market-driven sectors, while NGCP operates as a regulated natural monopoly strictly confined to transmission.

Accordingly, NGCP proposes treating these BESS facilities as regulated transmission assets rather than market participants. However, charging batteries during low-demand periods and discharging power into the grid during peak shortages or evening ramps closely mirrors energy arbitrage and generation/ancillary supply, functions traditionally reserved for private generation companies and independent BESS developers.

PIPPA and PSSEA emphasize that because NGCP is a regulated utility, classifying a P59.5 billion (or eventually P700 billion) battery fleet as transmission infrastructure allows NGCP to include the capital costs in its regulatory asset base (RAB). Rate-basing guarantees NGCP a regulated return on investment paid directly by electricity consumers through transmission wheeling charges, shifting financial and utilization risks away from private investors and onto ratepayers.

Private power producers, many of whom are already building utility-scale BESS or complying with the DOE’s mandate requiring new variable renewable plants (10 MW and above) to pair at least 20% capacity with storage, face direct competition from a monopoly operator that controls grid dispatch and enjoys guaranteed cost recovery.

Consequently, while neither group disputes the technical value of battery storage, both argue that NGCP’s monopoly-led ownership model fails to solve high power costs, undermines market competition, and risks passing massive regulated charges onto Filipino consumers. In other words, their clash with NGCP centers on governance, accountability, and cost protection as in who ultimately bears the financial risk and cost of building energy storage.

For the PIPPA and PSSEA, true protection against high electricity bills lies in enforcing EPIRA’s market boundaries, completing delayed transmission backbones, and definitely not through rate-based monopoly spending but by letting open competition to deliver the energy storage solutions the country needs. – Rappler.com

A veteran stock market analyst, Den Somera has long years of professional experience in investment banking and stockbroking and founder-convenor of The Monday Circle. You may reach the writer at kapitaltek@gmail.com
