articles.title: Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'
articles.summary: Funding from wealthy countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change hasn't materialized, says Uganda's environment minister. The East African country is hoping oil and carbon credits will…

image.caption: 'We are here begging for funds that are not forthcoming,' Beatrice Atim Anywar, Uganda's environment minister, told DWImage: DW

blocks.text: Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.

"This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation. "People are displaced, people are dying of harm, hunger. It has implications on food security and livelihoods."

In recent years, the East African nation has been hit by a series of climate-related disasters, from deadly landslides and floods washing away villages, to droughts damaging harvests and hydroelectricity production.
"When we come to COP and we talk of what the reality is on the ground, we Ugandans have suffered it," Anywar said, referring to the effects of climate change.
"It has an implication for the health of our people, on national budgets," she added.

blocks.caption: People search for missing belongings buried under landslides triggered by heavy rainfall in Kaptang village in Uganda in October 2025Image: Abubaker Lubowa/REUTERS

blocks.text: Climate financing for developing countries to deal with the impacts of a warming planet has become a major sticking point at this year's climate talks. The gathering of some 200 states is seeking to close gaps on how to scale up financing from developed states and whether support should be provided through grants or loans.
Africa contributes less than 4% of the global greenhouse emissions that drive rising temperatures globally, but the continent is among the most vulnerable to climate impacts.
Ramping up electricity production
As it deals with the affects of climate change, including extreme weather, Uganda is also rapidly expanding investment in electricity production from renewables such as hydropower and solar.

In the country of some 53 million people, more than 90% of Ugandan households still rely on wood and charcoal as the most affordable fuel for things like cooking. Biomass accounts for 90% of the country's final energy consumption.

While using wood and charcoal leads to deforestation, Ugandans have little choice. Only around 2% of the country's energy comes from electricity — which is largely derived from hydropower — and less than half of the population has access to electricity.

"Now we are deliberately going into scaling up the production of electricity — hydropower electricity — and making it cheaper for cooking," Anywar said. "We have other alternative energy sources... to mitigate this charcoal use. But the use needs to be phased out in a systematic manner by giving them alternatives."
As pipeline nears finish, resistance in Uganda holds firm
Drilling for oil

At the same time, the country is seeking to boost economic development by becoming an oil producer. Due to open in 2027, a controversial 1,443-kilometer (897-mile) pipeline is nearly complete. It connects two oil sites in eastern Uganda with a port on the Tanzanian coast.

Environmentalists have criticized the East African Crude Oil Pipeline project, which can transport up to 246,000 barrels per day. Environmentalists say it runs counter to the goal of limiting global temperature rise and could damage fragile ecosystems.
The Climate Accountability Institute said it would release 379 million tons of climate-heating pollution over its 20-year lifetime.
Oil wells for the project, operated by French energy giant TotalEnergies, are also located in Uganda's largest and oldest national park, Murchison Falls.

"That has been also a sticky issue. And actually, that is one of the challenges we are facing at COPs," Anywar said. She stressed that measures have been taken to limit emissions, and that the project was progressing in a "very deliberate way."

blocks.caption: Climate activists in New York protesting JP Morgan Chase bank's support of Total Energies East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP), which is displacing farmers in Uganda and TanzaniaImage: picture alliance / ZUMAPRESS.com

blocks.text: The minister also urged developed countries to cut less wealthy nations some slack for using the resources they have to drive much-needed development, saying oil revenues could help fund the transition to cleaner energy.

"You cannot tell us to cut off the umbilical cord that feeds us, as much as it has to be cut off," Anywar said, criticizing the lack of financing from developed countries to deal with climate change. "We are here begging for funds that are not forthcoming."
Anywar added that developing countries "need a just transition," referring to an equitable shift away from fossil fuels that focuses on protecting workers and communities.
Carbon trading 'breakthrough?'
Another way Uganda is looking to finance climate change adaptation is through carbon credits, Anywar said, describing them as a potential "breakthrough."

Carbon credits are tradeable permits representing one ton of carbon dioxide that has been reduced or removed from the atmosphere through initiatives such as forest protection, renewable energy projects or tree planting schemes. Companies or governments can buy them to offset emissions they have not cut themselves.
"Our country is rich with biodiversity. And that is what we are looking forward to — attracting investors into our natural setup so that we earn some finances," Anywar said.

blocks.caption: Uganda is rich in biodiversity, including lush tropical forests with plenty of wildlifeImage: C. Kaiser/blickwinkel/picture alliance

blocks.text: Carbon credits have been promoted as an important source of income for developing countries. But they have also faced criticism, for a lack of transparency and allowing polluting activities to continue.

"We need to have a bankable approach to all interventions. Otherwise… it's not going to work for us," Anywar said, adding that her country also wants to attract investment and build partnerships in smart agriculture and the energy transition.
"If we rely on begging for funds which are not forthcoming, we shall go back empty handed."
This interview also appeared as a video.

articles.title: Prison authorities consider whether Russell Brand YouTube message breached rules on victim distress
articles.summary:
Ministry of Justice weighs video read out by Brand’s wife as Burnham urges YouTube to remove it

The prison authorities are weighing up whether Russell Brand harassed his victims by issuing…

blocks.text: The prison authorities are weighing up whether Russell Brand harassed his victims by issuing comments through his wife insisting he was not guilty of rape and sexual assault.

After Andy Burnham called on Google to take down the statement from YouTube, a continuing Ministry of Justice inquiry is focusing on whether Brand has broken rules that are supposed to prevent “serious distress” to the victims of crime.
Other factors that will help to decide whether he has broken a rule include the “notoriety” of the crimes and the length of time between the verdict and the statement.
A video in which Brand’s wife, Laura Gallacher, read out a message from the jailed sex offender protesting he was not guilty has remained on YouTube days after ministers asked for it to be removed.
Brand is serving a 10-and-a-half-year term after he was convicted of one count of rape and three sexual assaults at Southwark crown court on 5 November.

On Thursday night, the UK prime minister said he “wouldn’t leap” to changing the law to force social media companies to take down the content. But he added: “I would call on those social media companies to take these interviews down.
“You know, why are we having to hear from from him? We shouldn’t be, and certainly [the victims] shouldn’t be hearing from him.”

According to official guidance on prisoner access to the media, a prison governor must decide whether to permit it, and must consider that “serious distress to victims of the prisoner and/or outrage to public sensibilities is not likely to result from the broadcast. This is likely to occur if, for example, the prisoner’s crimes or conduct are recent, notorious or horrific.”

The rules state that correspondence likely to be published or broadcast “must not contain material about the prisoner’s own crime or past offences or those of others, except where it consists of serious representations about conviction or sentence”.

It is understood that the inquiry is taking into account the right of prisoners to protest their innocence. However, there is a strict protocol governing the way such statements are issued and whether permission has been sought beforehand.
Recent reports have claimed that Brand, who is jailed in the category C HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, is likely to be moved to a category A or B prison instead after protesting his innocence.
It is understood that there has been no such proposal, and he is likely to remain in Littlehey, a specialist prison for sex offenders.
The government has no power to compel YouTube’s direct owner, Google, to remove the video, but has been in “dialogue” with the tech firm over it.

“We trust that they will do the right thing,” a Downing Street spokesperson said when asked about the standoff. They said: “The prime minister’s position on this is that Russell Brand’s victims deserve peace, and we’ve heard enough from him.
after newsletter promotion

“We’ve asked YouTube to remove the content. I would also just point out that they acted before when they suspended Brand’s account from making money. Given he has been convicted of rape by a jury of his peers, we trust that they will act again.”

No 10 was repeatedly asked whether Burnham would personally welcome the video being removed, as well as Brand’s YouTube channel being disabled. It told reporters: “Removal ultimately depends on YouTube and the platform’s terms and conditions.”

A spokesperson for Google said: “We’re aware of the new content and our teams are investigating. We suspended Russell Brand’s channel from the YouTube partner programme in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then.”
Kemi Badenoch said if she was in power she would not immediately demand Google remove the video.

The Conservative leader told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “My personal opinion is that Russell Brand has been convicted. He is guilty under the law. His wife is a separate person. She can make the protestations that she likes.

“I think that immediately demanding the private platforms take things down without looking at exactly whether a law has been broken is not where I would start from. If we want to make legislation for that, then we can look at that.”

articles.title: Petition asks Netflix to cancel The Body for 'blasphemous' and 'anti-Christian' content
articles.summary: The new Netflix show The Body is garnering backlash for being "blasphemous" and "anti-Christian," with over 110,000 people signing a petition asking Netflix to cancel the show. The Body, which…

image.caption: The cast of Netflix's The Body, from left: Michela Luci as Amy, Emily Roman as Claire, Kyra Pierce as Bailey, Sarah Abbot as Olivia, Geena Meszaros as Lisbeth, Phallon Pierce as Brit, Bella Neuspiel as Katie and Julia Lowe as Blair. (Netflix)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

The new Netflix show The Body is garnering backlash for being "blasphemous" and "anti-Christian," with over 110,000 people signing a petition asking Netflix to cancel the show. The Body, which released on the streaming platform on Nov. 11, is a coming-of-age drama by writer, actor and director Quinn Shephard that tells the story of a dance team at a Catholic school.
The petition to cancel the coming-of-age drama has reached over 110,000 signatures so far
The new Netflix show The Body is taking heat for being "blasphemous" and "anti-Christian," with more than 110,000 people signing a petition calling on the streaming giant to cancel the show.
The Body, which released on Netflix on Nov. 11, is a coming-of-age drama by writer, actor and director Quinn Shephard. It tells the story of a dance team at a Catholic school.

In the show, the girls perform a mock satanic ritual at a Halloween party, pretending to offer one of their classmates as a virgin sacrifice. Afterward, the girls begin having prophetic visions, sparking hysteria in their town.
The petition on CitizenGO calls it: "A blasphemous anti-Christian series featuring satanic ritual."
"Parents cannot screen every show teens press play on. Netflix is counting on that," it says.
As of publication, the eight-episode series is third in Netflix Canada's top 10. According to Variety, it drew 5.1 million views in its first five days in the U.S.

The petition was launched before the show's premiere and initially called on Netflix not to release it. As of Nov. 19, just over a week after the show was released, it had received more than 118,000 signatures.
The petition also criticized Netflix's marketing campaign for posting photos portraying the show's characters as saints.
Not the first program protested

The petition also criticizes previous Netflix releases, including The First Temptation of Christ — a Brazilian comedy released in 2019 — for mocking Jesus. It also mentions the 2020 French drama Cuties, saying it "sexualized eleven-year-old girls."
Despite protests, streaming platforms rarely respond by removing content from their libraries.

In 2019, more than 20,000 people signed a petition to cancel the series Good Omens, claiming it mocked God and normalized Satanism. However, protesters mistakenly addressed their petition to Netflix rather than Amazon, which produced the series. Good Omens went on to have a second and third season.

In 2021, about 100 Netflix employees staged a protest outside the company's headquarters in Los Angeles over Dave Chappelle's comedy special, The Closer. Protesters said the special was transphobic. Netflix kept the special available on its platform.

The animated sitcom South Park has also faced numerous controversies involving various groups, including Christians, Muslims, Mormons and the Trump administration. The series is now in its 29th season.
CBC reached out to Netflix for comment on the petition but did not receive a response before publication. Netflix has yet to confirm whether the series will be renewed for a second season.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Philip Drost is a network senior writer for CBC News based in Fredericton. You can reach him at philip.drost@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Canada seeking interim trade arrangement with U.S. by end of year: sources

image.caption: Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc met with advisory committee members on Thursday about the state of negotiations with the Trump administration. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Canada is seeking to reach an interim tariff arrangement with the Trump administration by the end of the year, rather than a full trade deal, sources tell CBC News.
Negotiators seeking relief on steel, aluminum, auto, lumber and other sectors
· CBC News
· Posted: Nov 19, 2026 2:04 PM EST | Last Updated: 18 minutes ago
Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc met with the federal government's Canada-U.S economic advisory committee on Thursday.

Sources with knowledge of the meeting said that the government's goal to reach an interim agreement, rather than a permanent new deal, would cover Section 232 tariffs on steel, aluminum, auto and lumber — as well as Section 338 tariffs imposed on Canadian goods in August after previous talks broke down.
Prime Minister Mark Carney is heading back to Ottawa after a nine-day trade mission to Europe and Asia.

items: 'If the U.S. doesn't want to do a deal, we're busy,' Carney says
Canada's trade with China isn't U.S. president's top concern: Carney

blocks.text: Speaking virtually to the Dealbook summit from China on Wednesday, Carney said Canada continues "to have a series of issues" when it comes to trade with the U.S.
The prime minister indicated that there had been progress toward an agreement in recent weeks but said they're not at the point of putting anything to paper.

Carney met with U.S. President Donald Trump in China on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit — a conversation he described as "reasonably direct" but one that didn't produce a trade breakthrough.

During his latest trip, Carney brokered free trade deals with the Philippines and the 11-nation ASEAN bloc — and secured meaningful market access for Canadian commodities in return for allowing a relatively small number of Chinese EVs to be imported at lower tariff rates and adjustments to import rules for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products.
"We'd like to do a deal. If the U.S. doesn't want to do a deal, we're busy," Carney told the summit's audience in New York.

He holds a master's degree in journalism and a bachelor's degree in public affairs and policy management, both from Carleton University. articles.title: Man arrested after ‘horrific’ knife attack on Bradford councillor
articles.summary:
Politicians call attack on independent councillor Ibrar Ali canvassing in Bradford Moor ward ‘deeply disturbing’

Politicians have described an attack on a councillor who was canvassing in…
articles.byline: Robyn Vinter North of England correspondent

blocks.text: Politicians have described an attack on a councillor who was canvassing in Bradford as “horrific” and “deeply disturbing”, after a man was arrested on suspicion of attempted murder.

A 32-year-old man is in custody suspected of attacking Ibrar Ali at about 11am on Thursday as the independent councillor was door-knocking in his Bradford Moor ward, leaving him with a stab wound in the leg.
West Yorkshire police said there was nothing to suggest the incident was politically motivated, although the investigation was at an early stage.
Jim McMahon, the MP for Oldham West, described the attack as “horrific” and said: “Our thoughts are with [Ali], his family, councillors in Bradford and, of course, our members of parliament too.
“Our thoughts are very much with you all at this time.”
Imran Hussain, the MP for Bradford East, said: “This horrific attack is deeply disturbing. My thoughts and prayers are with councillor Ibrar Ali and his family.

“No elected politician should feel under threat or fear for their safety while carrying out their duties and serving their community. I am receiving regular updates from the police as they deal with this extremely serious incident, and I understand a suspect is in police custody.”
Officers were called just after 11am to reports that a 52-year-old man, a serving Bradford councillor, had been found seriously injured on Manse Street.

Police said: “The man is believed to have first been injured on Thornbury Avenue, before being driven to Manse Street where emergency services attended. He was taken to hospital where his condition is described as serious but not life-threatening.”

blocks.caption: A police forensic officer investigates the scene of the knife attack in Bradford. Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/Getty Images

blocks.text: A 32-year-old man fled to the roof of a property on Thornbury Avenue but was brought down some time later and arrested on suspicion of attempted murder.
He remains in custody.

Sharon Taylor, a local government minister, named Ali in the House of Lords. Lady Taylor said: “I am afraid I have to mention a very tragic incident that’s occurred in Bradford … where an independent councillor who was out canvassing has been stabbed.

“I would want to send the wishes, that I’m sure noble lords would agree, of the whole house to councillor Ibrar Ali for a speedy recovery, and our thoughts are with all of those in Bradford who are affected by this awful incident.”
Police cordons were in place on Manse Street, Leeds Road and Thornbury Avenue while inquiries are carried out.

Adam, who works in the area and did not want to give his surname, said: “I know the councillor on a personal level and it’s shocking. I just know he’s a very kind, warm-hearted man whose goal is to serve, his life is to help out everyone.
“He just wants everyone to succeed. He definitely didn’t deserve what’s happened.
“The world’s not a nice place.”
Chris Herd, the lord mayor of Bradford, said: “It is deeply distressing that this incident has occurred.
“Councillors work tirelessly on behalf of residents across the district and should be able to carry out their duties safely.

“We will continue to work closely with our colleagues at West Yorkshire police as they investigate this matter and seek to bring those responsible to justice, and would like to thank those who provided aid and support at the time.”
Press Association contributed to this report

articles.title: Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
articles.summary: European allies of Ukraine say they have a "united" negotiating position at a summit in Berlin.
articles.byline: Jaroslav Lukiv, Laura Gozzi, Paul Kirby

blocks.text: European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.

US President Donald Trump's envoys were also there, and his son-in-law Jared Kushner said Trump wanted to make a deal with Russia "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US led peace talks.
Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.

In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.
Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."

But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".
Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".

Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition. Russia has never accepted the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but Article Five-style guarantees could theoretically be offered to Kyiv without being part of the Western defensive alliance.

Zelensky and the three European leaders - Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron - were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."

The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".
"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.

There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, Witkoff and Kushner appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table.

But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
While Russia has engaged with several rounds of talks over the last year, little in Moscow's rhetoric or actions suggests that the Kremlin is considering scaling down its war on Ukraine.

It continues to pound Kyiv's energy infrastructure to cripple it as winter takes hold, increasing numbers of civilian casualties are being recorded across the country, and Kremlin officials haven't budged from Russia's demands for Ukraine sovereign territory.

As delegations were meeting in China and Germany on Thursday, several buildings in Kyiv's historic centre came under attack from drones. One person was killed in a strike on a residential building in the Podilskyi neighbourhood, while the Dutch and Austrian embassies as well as Saint Volodymyr's Cathedral reported damage.
And today, Putin vowed that Moscow's response to a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge linking Russia with occupied Crimea would be "considerably more painful" than what Kyiv had achieved.
He also said he had discussed a "possible ceasefire in a number of areas" but had decided against it after the attack on the bridge.
Still, Putin claimed to be "interested" in ending the war and was ready for making compromises, while Ukraine and Europe were not.
"I assure you, we have no desire at all to continue this armed conflict," Putin said.

articles.title: UK and EU plan first talks on sending refused asylum seekers to third countries
articles.summary:
Two sides to commit to discussing third-country hubs as part of reset pact after five-country deal with Rwanda

The UK and the EU plan to establish formal talks for the first time about…

blocks.text: The UK and the EU plan to establish formal talks for the first time about sending rejected asylum seekers to third-country hubs, according to a leaked document.

A draft of a joint statement expected to be signed by Andy Burnham and Ursula von der Leyen at a summit on Friday morning states that both sides will establish “a structured dialogue” to discuss “returns to third countries”.
Until now, the Home Office has been seeking bilateral agreements with third countries allowing the removal of migrants, but with no obvious success.
Last week, five EU countries – Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands – announced an agreement in principle with Rwanda to establish a migrant “return hub” there in 2027.

Burnham hinted at possible cooperation with EU countries last week when he told reporters that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that [the five-country deal] with interest, learning from what went on in the past”. He said: “The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”
The UK has been fighting for deeper cooperation with the EU on migration, with the new deal on a “strategic dialogue” secured in the last two weeks by negotiators in Brussels.

It is a key part of the UK-EU reset pact, which also covers a youth mobility scheme, tariffs on Chinese imports, food and drink exports to the EU and a wider restatement of commitment on defence and security.
Informed sources confirmed this was the first time the UK and the EU had agreed to “open a dialogue on returns” after the launch of the bloc’s Channel action plan in June this year.
Whitehall sources said the UK was now open to the possibility of sending rejected claimants to Rwanda – a recent pivot from the position under Keir Starmer’s government, which rejected the move.
According to a draft of the joint agreement, negotiations over third-country hubs will be part of increased cooperation to tackle irregular migration.

The document states: “The EU and UK … will establish a structured dialogue on migration covering in particular the joint activities under the Channel action plan, action against irregular migration and migrant smuggling networks, strategic communication and border management, upstream cooperation and engagement with third countries, returns to third countries, pull factors for irregular migrants and legal pathway.”
In May, the UK and 45 other European countries signed an agreement that explicitly endorsed plans to send unwanted asylum seekers to third-country hubs.

A political declaration from the 46 members of the Council of Europe, the body that oversees the European convention on human rights (ECHR), said states had an “undeniable sovereign right” to control their borders.

It is understood that the UK has been seeking a deal with an unnamed third country, similar to the Italy-Albania agreement that allowed Rome to place detention centres in Albania. Albania has ruled out a bilateral agreement on a return hub with the UK.

Previous discussions have reportedly centred on 11 countries: Armenia, Egypt, Ethiopia, Ghana, Libya, Mauritania, Rwanda, Senegal, Tunisia, Uganda and Uzbekistan. Montenegro has denied reports that it is considering housing refused asylum seekers.
Starmer scrapped a Tory plan to forcibly send small-boat arrivals to Rwanda where their asylum claims would have been processed.

Before the election, the Conservative government had spent £700m on its Rwanda returns policy, which was meant to deter Channel crossings. The scheme hit legal and political obstacles from the start, with the UK supreme court eventually ruling it illegal.

Under Burnham, the Home Office has refused to close down the possibility of sending asylum seekers to Rwanda. This week, when asked if the UK might ever send asylum seekers to Rwanda, a Home Office spokesperson said: “The UK, like other European countries, is exploring innovative approaches including returns hubs to tackle illegal migration.”
The UK has been looking for years to strengthen cooperation with France and other EU member states to tackle small boats carrying asylum seekers across the Channel.

But sources say it is only in recent months that there has been a change of mood in the EU, with member states realising that the intensity of criminal trafficking across the Channel is “proving [to be] a pull factor” to enter the EU. Those that fail to make it to British shores remain in the EU’s migrant support system.

Responding to the planned cooperation on migrant hubs, Madeleine Sumption, the head of the Migration Observatory at Oxford University, said: “Its inclusion in the statement would confirm the now relatively widespread interest in ‘third country’ options.”
In response, Imran Hussain, the director of external affairs at the Refugee Council, said return hubs were likely to be difficult and costly to run.
“Removing people to places they have never stepped foot will be difficult and distressing,” he said.
“The last decade has shown that working with people to support their return to their countries is far more successful.”

A Home Office spokesperson said: “While we are not part of this EU member state initiative, there is widespread international agreement on the need to have practical and workable solutions to deal with the global challenge of illegal migration.

“We continue to explore innovative approaches, including returns hubs, to build on the 80,000 people with no right to be in the UK returned or deported since July 2024. We have consistently made clear that we support the principle of returns hubs.”

articles.title: Germany news: Pistorius visits Auschwitz memorial in Poland trip
articles.summary: Germany's defense minister's first stop in Poland was the memorial site of the former Nazi extermination camp Auschwitz-Birkenau. Follow DW for more.

image.caption: Auschwitz-Birkenau is one of the biggest symbols of the Holocaust and Germany's Nazi regimeImage: Alex Pantcykov/dpa/Sputnik/picture-alliance

blocks.text: November 19, 2026
German defense minister call Auschwitz a 'warning' to all of us

blocks.caption: Pistorius said Auschwitz provides a warning of what must not be allowed to happenImage: Fabian Sommer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius on Thursday called on Europeans to be vigilant against far-right extremism and warned of divisions and labels in society.
Speaking during a visit to Auschwitz-Birkenau, a former concentration camp, Pistorius said the site bore witness to the worst of Nazi Germany's crimes, calling it an absolute low point.

"It all started with defining what made a life unworthy; by dividing according to race, origin, faith, sexual orientation," Pistorius warned, saying that such marginalization was experiencing a "renaissance" and "gaining ground with far-right extremist parties across Europe."
The defense minister said Auschwitz provides all people, but particularly Germans, with a "symbol warning that we all bear responsibility for what happens and what must not be allowed to happen."
During his tour of the camp, Pistorius laid a wreath at its death wall, where Nazi soldiers shot roughly 5,000 prisoners dead, and lit a candle at the victims' memorial.
Before he departed the site, Pistorius expressed his wish that more German students and travel groups would visit the camp "than appears to be the case at present."

articles.title: Iraq's risky standoff: The state vs. Iran-allied militias
articles.summary: This week, Iraqi security forces surrounded an area run by the Kataib Hezbollah militia. Onlookers describe it as the most dangerous confrontation between the Iraqi state and Iran-allied militias in…

image.caption: The Iraqi state has been trying to disarm local militia groups and some have agreed to give up their arms; Kataib Hezbollah is not one of themImage: Murtadha Al-Sudani/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: For years, there have all kinds of rumors about Jurf al-Sakhar, an area around 50 kilometers (31 miles) south of the Iraqi capital Baghdad. It is controlled by an Iraqi militia called Kataib Hezbollah, that's closely allied with Iran, and no Iraqi government troops or news media outlets have been allowed inside for around 12 years.

Rumors about what's happening in the area include allegations about secret prisons, mass graves, drone and weapons manufacturing and storage, as well as criminal activity such as oil smuggling. Jurf al-Sakhar is also allegedly a base for foreign, Hezbollah-supporting nationals from Iran, Yemen, Bahrain and Lebanon.
Recently two people — an Israeli researcherand a US journalist — who were kidnapped by an Iraqi militia are thought to have been held captive in this area.

blocks.caption: The Kataib Hezbollah militia, first founded around 2007, entered Jurf al-Sakhar in 2014, as part of the fight against the 'Islamic State' groupImage: Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Jurf al-Sakhar previously had an estimated 89,000 residents but after the extremist group known as the "Islamic State," or IS, rose to power in Iraq in 2014, much of the population was displaced in fighting. The area was eventually taken over by Kataib Hezbollah, a militia that had fought IS alongside other armed groups.

As a collective, the armed groups are referred to as the Popular Mobilization Forces, or PMF. Not all of them have pledged allegiance to Iran but Kataib Hezbollah, a Shiite Muslim majority group, has.
In the past 12 years, tens of thousands of the displaced people from here, mostly Sunni Muslims, have not been allowed to return and the area has been described as militarized.
Its name was even changed by Kataib Hezbollah fighters, from Jurf al-Sakhar ("rocky bank") to Jurf al-Nasr ("bank of victory").
'Not even over our dead bodies'
But recent events may shake Kataib Hezbollah's hold on this area.

An early November report for the Iraqi government says that since 2021, the group has smuggled hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of state-owned oil, siphoned from pipelines around Jurf al-Sakhar.
Kataib Hezbollah denies this.
Iraq's new government, headed by Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, made several arrests based on the report and demanded that Kataib Hezbollah leave Jurf al-Sakhar by Friday, Nov. 20.
Kataib Hezbollah rejected al-Zaidi's ultimatum, with a spokesperson saying the group would not withdraw "not even over our dead bodies."
Al-Zaidi then ordered state security forces to surround the area, while Hezbollah reportedly brought in reinforcements.

blocks.caption: Comments on social media indicate many Iraqis approve of their prime minister's reasons for the standoff: They believe their oil is being stolen to benefit foreigners Image: Hadi Mizban/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Observers have described the standoff as one of the most consequential and riskiest confrontations between an Iraqi government and Iranian-backed militiasin Iraq in more than two decades.

"It is a political signal that things will change, that he [al-Zaidi] wants to disarm militias, integrate them into state and claim back the state's authority," Ulf Laessing, head of the Syria and Iraq project for Germany's Konrad Adenauer Foundation, or KAS, told DW. "But it's a minefield and he needs to navigate carefully."

The standoff is also the result of long-running political tensions in Iraq, where the state is torn between its US allies on the one hand and Iranian allies on the other. Both hold sway in Iraq and are considered important relationships.

During Donald Trump's presidency of the US, and thanks to the US and Israel's war with Iran, there's been more pressure on Iraq to disarm Iran's allies inside the country. Al-Zaidi has set a deadline of next June to bring all weapons under the state's control.
Tensions, fears grow

The situation in Jurf al-Sakhar became even more tense this week. Al-Zaidi announced a new security plan for the area that involves other members of the PMF, state security forces and the police. Kataib Hezbollah rejected the plan.

"Al-Zaidi appears serious about ending Kataib Hezbollah's autonomous control of Jurf al-Sakhar," Hayder al-Shakeri, a research fellow at the British think tank Chatham House told DW. "Deploying federal forces and now establishing a new security command there shows this has moved beyond rhetoric."

But how dangerous is Kataib Hezbollah really? After all, al-Zaidi was actually nominated for the prime minister's job by a political bloc known as the Coalition Framework, or CF — these are the politicians who represent the PMF in parliament. Kataib Hezbollah's political party, Harakat Huqooq, is part of the CF.

And other researchers have been critical on social media, noting that the PMF troops that will be given partial control over Jurf al-Sakhar (should Kataib Hezbollah withdraw) are associated with that group anyway.

But Iraqi news media have also reported that there are divisions inside the CF, and apparently even within Kataib Hezbollah, about how to deal with the current standoff. Reportedly, some senior officials think that parts of Jurf al-Sakhar could be handed to federal forces in a gradual withdrawal, the London-based outlet Amwaj Media reported earlier this week, while some senior members of Kataib Hezbollah would seemingly prefer to hand the territory over to certain PMF brigades rather than to state security forces.
What will happen next?

Late Thursday afternoon, the news agency Reuters reported that, according to three anonymous officials, all parties had come to an agreement that would allow government forces to enter Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday.
A compromise is good because it avoids violence, KAS' Laessing said. "It might not be what al-Zaidi initially hoped for but it's still a political signal."

blocks.caption: Iraqi PM Ali al-Zaidi (left) in the US in summer 2026: The US has warned Iraq it could be treated as a state sponsor of terrorism if it misses next year's deadline to disarm militiasImage: Eugene Oliver/DoD/Planet Pix/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: If it did come to actual fighting, the Iraqi military has more resources than Kataib Hezbollah, al-Shakeri explained. "[It] could probably take Jurf al-Sakhar if the political leadership and security institutions remained united," he said. "But there would be no easy victory. Kataib Hezbollah does not need to defeat the Iraqi army conventionally. It can impose costs through asymmetric attacks, political pressure and its networks inside the state."

How the reported compromise plays out in the coming days, will also impact other Iraqi militias and they will be watching closely. Because "the core issue is whether a faction can continue controlling territory and economic activity beyond effective government oversight," al-Shakeri explained.

"The most likely compromise may be to remove Kataib Hezbollah's monopoly rather than remove the PMF from Jurf al-Sakhar altogether," he continued. "That would still matter if it opened the area to regular state forces, if it protects the oil infrastructure and places security under a clearer government command structure."
It could also lead to displaced residents being allowed back to their homes.

"But if one PMF faction simply replaces another while retaining its own networks and autonomy, then Zaidi has redistributed armed influence rather than fundamentally resolved the problem," al-Shakeri concluded.

articles.title: Alberta government to revise policy as school boards say new flag regulations could cost millions of dollars
articles.summary: Alberta’s education and childcare minister says he will change an incoming school flags regulation that has school divisions collectively preparing to spend millions of dollars on hundreds of new…

image.caption: The Alberta government passed the Flag Display Regulation this fall, requiring schools to fly both the Alberta and Canada flags on separate flagpoles during the school year. (Collin Gallant/CBC)

blocks.text: Edmonton

Alberta’s education and childcare minister says he will change an incoming school flags regulation that has school divisions collectively preparing to spend millions of dollars on hundreds of new outdoor flagpoles.
Education minister says he'll change an incoming school flags regulation
Alberta’s education minister says he will change an incoming school flags regulation that has school boards collectively preparing to spend millions of dollars on hundreds of new outdoor flagpoles.

On Thursday, Education and Childcare Minister Demetrios Nicolaides told reporters at the legislature that school boards buying new flagpoles should “pause until we’re able to provide some additional direction."
Nicolaides has also said he believes the money would be better spent by directing it to classrooms.

A flag display regulation, made public in late October to accompany new legislation from last spring, says schools must fly the Canada and Alberta flags outside their buildings and on separate poles to satisfy national flag protocol.
The provincial regulation says any work needed to ensure the flags fly on separate poles is supposed to be done by Jan. 4, 2027.

items: New provincial flag rules will cost southern Alberta school board thousands of dollars, superintendent says

blocks.text: CBC News reached out to eight school divisions to ask about how many of their schools have just one flagpole and how much money they anticipated they would need to spend to satisfy the provincial regulation.

The Calgary Board of Education, the province’s most populous school division, counted 223 schools and leased sites with a single flagpole. Spokesperson Joanne Anderson said in a Wednesday email that the division estimated it would cost $4 million to install a second pole on every site. The regulation says that work is supposed to be done by Jan. 4, 2027.

items: New regulations on flags flown at Alberta schools to take effect in January

blocks.text: “We will not be able to meet the Jan. 4 outdoor flag installation requirement as we will need to procure and install the flags and flagpoles,” Anderson said in an email.
Calgary’s Catholic school division said 122 schools would need a second flagpole, and each pole could cost $20,000 to $30,000 to purchase and install.

In Northland School Division, which has locations across northern Alberta, 12 schools would need additional flagpoles, and each would cost at least $20,000, spokesperson Curtis Walty said in an email.
“Meeting the Jan. 4, 2027, deadline would be impossible,” his email said. “Installing additional flagpoles would place significant pressure on education funding.”
Edmonton Public Schools said more than 170 sites would need a second flagpole, and 77 Edmonton Catholic Schools would need a second flagpole. Neither provided cost estimates.

The Fort McMurray Public School Division plans to install wall-mounted flagpoles on some schools that cost $2,000 each as a temporary measure, before installing permanent flagpoles in the ground next summer, a statement said.
Opposition raises lack of consultation

The issue came to a head at a meeting of the Alberta School Boards Association (ASBA) in Edmonton earlier this week, where members passed a resolution calling on the government to suspend the flags regulation, restore school board authority over flag displays and eliminate the mandatory costs for installing flags and poles.
Smith attended a breakfast event with trustees in Edmonton Tuesday and held a fireside chat with ASBA president Shali Baziuk.

items: Alberta government to delay adopting new limits on flags at schools

blocks.text: NDP MLA Janis Irwin said she was at the meeting and heard the exchanges.

On Tuesday, she told reporters she believes the premier seemed to be unaware of the costs and challenges of installing flagpoles because her government fails to consult with affected people before introducing new rules.
“It should have been a wake-up call for her to recognize that she's making decisions without understanding the consequences on the ground," Irwin said.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith speaks to the media in Calgary on Oct. 21, 2026. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)
Baziuk declined an interview request Wednesday.
Smith was asked about the ASBA meeting in question period at the legislature on Wednesday.
"Admittedly, we didn't know that it is common to only have one flagpole at a school," she said.
Changes coming, minister says

CBC News requested interviews with eight school board chairs on Wednesday. Although all declined, Fort McMurray Public School Division chair Tim O’Hara said in a statement that he appreciated the premier’s willingness to listen and "her recognition that 'You don’t know what you don’t know,' as she stated in response to finding out how many schools exist with less than the newly required two flagpoles.”
O’Hara said the event highlights why meaningful exchanges with school boards are important to identify practical obstacles before the government introduces legislation and proclaims it into law.
Nicolaides also met with ASBA members in Edmonton, but on Monday.
On Wednesday, Nicolaides told reporters at the legislature he would be changing the regulations.
Education Minister Demetrios Nicolaides says he will review new school flags regulations after school trustees said hundreds of buildings need a second flagpole to fulfil the incoming rules. (CBC)
He said he would consider removing the requirement for the Canada and Alberta flags to be displayed outside schools, but didn’t have more details on what the changes would entail.
“We don't want school boards to be absorbing these kinds of significant costs,” Nicolaides said.
Flag protocols could dictate costs

Gary Komusi, a Calgary business owner who runs Signs Talk, installs and repairs flagpoles as part of his work. In an interview with CBC News, he said following national protocol around the Canadian flag prompts some limitations around how a school could fly a second flag.
For example, he said if the Canadian flag is flying alongside an Alberta flag, the Canadian flag must be on the left-hand side and on a taller pole.

The height of the pole each school requires would depend on what their existing pole is like, Komusi said. Once ordered, a pole could take six to eight weeks to arrive, he added, potentially making the Jan. 4 deadline impossible to meet.
Komusi said the cost would depend on the length of the flagpole and the time of year it is installed, but he estimates it would be at least $5,000 per flag.
Installers would have to pour a cement footing with metal components for each flagpole base, then erect the pole onto it.
Flags themselves aren’t expensive, Komusi said, but schools have to ensure the Canadian flag is the correct dimensions — twice as wide as it is long.
Komusi said he is sympathetic to schools that have to spend money to meet the requirements.

“I'm not looking at this as a windfall for Signs Talk, or the flag industry, which I guess it is, but it's a hardship on the schools,” he said. “If this all went away, that would probably be for the best.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Janet French covers the Alberta Legislature for CBC Edmonton. She previously spent 15 years working at newspapers, including the Edmonton Journal and Saskatoon StarPhoenix. You can reach her at janet.french@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Victim's lawyers back closed testimony, stronger protection for Duterte ICC trial witnesses
articles.summary: PRAGUE, Czech Republic - Amid the “exceptional circumstances” in former President Rodrigo Duterte"s International Criminal Court (ICC) case, closed sessions and stronger protections for testifying…
articles.byline: Andy Peñafuerte III, Jay-vee Marasigan Pangan

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 1:56am

PRAGUE, Czech Republic – Amid the “exceptional circumstances” in former President Rodrigo Duterte’s International Criminal Court (ICC) case, closed sessions and stronger protections for testifying witnesses are necessary, the victims’ lawyers tell the Trial Chamber III.

While Common Legal Representatives of the Victims (CLRV) Gilbert Andres, Joel Butuyan, and Paolina Massidda back the Office of the Prosecutor’s request for in-court protective measures for victims and witnesses, they suggest the court adopt a “comprehensive and prospective approach” in its assessment.

In particular, the lawyers request the use of closed sessions “for all the testimony” of most witnesses, combined with pseudonyms and voice distortions for “effective protection,” given the “objectively justifiable risks” these individuals face.

“The pseudonym would prevent the formal identification of the witness in the proceedings, while closed session testimony would prevent the disclosure of the substantive and contextual details capable of revealing [REDACTED] identity,” the lawyers argued in their filing released on November 19.
Political and social context

The prosecution had earlier sought protective and special measures for 55 witnesses expected to testify in Duterte’s trial, including pseudonyms, face and voice distortion, private or closed sessions, and psychological support for some witnesses.

The victims’ lawyers said public hearings remain a fundamental principle at the ICC, but that openness must be balanced against the Court’s obligation to protect the safety, physical and psychological well-being, dignity and privacy of victims and witnesses.

Noting the “particular political and social context” of Duterte’s case, the CLRVs said conventional protective measures “do not necessarily eliminate the risk of identification,” particularly when details disclosed during testimony could reveal a witness’s identity.

The CLRVs also urged judges to consider risks to witnesses’ families, saying that in the Philippines’ “close-knit communities and family-oriented social context”, the consequences of identifying a witness could extend beyond the person testifying.

In another redacted section, the lawyers said public identification in the “prevailing political and social climate in the Philippines” could expose a witness to a “real risk of harm, intimidation and/or social ostracism.”
“Accordingly, in adjudicating the Request, the Chamber should consider not only the risks faced by the witness, but also the foreseeable repercussions [REDACTED] family.”
Participating victims and witnesses
The ICC’s page on Duterte’s case states that Trial Chamber III has authorized more than 500 victims to participate in the proceedings set to open on November 30.
“More victims may apply and be authorised to participate in the trial,” the page stated.
Victims and witnesses have different roles in ICC proceedings.

“Witnesses give evidence in Court to help establish the facts of a case. They may be eyewitnesses, people with inside knowledge, or experts. Victims could also be witnesses or be authorized by the judges to appear and present their own views before the Court.

Participating victims have suffered harm from crimes related to the case and have been granted the right to participate by the judges. Participating victims are represented by their own representative/lawyer in the courtroom, who represents their views and concerns.”

The ICC said its obligation to protect the safety, physical and psychological well-being, dignity and privacy of victims and witnesses starts from the investigation and continues throughout the proceedings.
“Intimidating or interfering with witnesses at any stage of the investigations or the proceedings can constitute an offence against the administration of justice at the ICC.”
The ICC also reminds the public that the identities of protected witnesses remain confidential and must be respected.
“Respecting witnesses means respecting the justice process.” — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: 'We could have been dead,' says tenant who escaped Cape Breton building collapse
articles.summary: Viola Baker says she was in bed Wednesday morning when she heard a big bang, and all of a sudden the walls started caving in. She rushed to help rescue her daughter and 15-year-old grandson.

image.caption: Viola Baker was a tenant in the building that collapsed and burned on Wednesday. (Kyle Moore/CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia
Viola Baker says she was in bed Wednesday morning when she heard a big bang, and all of a sudden the walls started caving in. She rushed to help rescue her daughter and 15-year-old grandson.
Viola Baker says she's amazed everyone survived the incident
A woman who survived an explosion and the collapse of her apartment building in Glace Bay, N.S., on Wednesday says she's amazed everyone survived.
An explosion rocked the building at 130 Commercial St. around 6 a.m., causing the collapse and fire.
The structure, which housed a pizza shop on the ground floor and apartments above, was destroyed.
Officials say all 24 people who lived in the building were accounted for, including 17 who had minor injuries.
Viola Baker was in bed around early Wednesday morning when she heard a big bang.
"That’s when everything started shaking and everything was all coming down," she said. "I didn't know what the hell was going on."
Baker said she could hear her daughter and 15-year-old grandson screaming for help, so she kicked their door open.
"When I got there, I opened up my eyes and said, 'Oh my god.' The whole front of the building was right in the room."
She said the fridge fell on top of her daughter and part of the roof and some pipes fell on her grandson's head.
The building at 130 Commercial St. in Glace Bay, N.S., was destroyed after an explosion and fire on Wednesday. (Ernie Bagnell)
Baker said a taxi driver helped them get out from the rubble.
She said she's grateful for the first responders and everyone who has helped her family and the other tenants.
"So help me God, I don’t know how anybody walked. I was so happy that we all did and that we all got out," she said.
"It could have been worse. We could have been dead."
Baker said in the aftermath of the incident on Wednesday she wasn't in pain, but on Thursday she has pain in her back and bruises have started to appear.
She said she has lost everything. Her grandson has been especially concerned about the loss of his Xbox, Nintendo Switch and his collection of 72 wrestler figurines.
"There's a lot of stuff that can be replaced, but their lives couldn't," Baker said of the tenants.
John Marr lived on the main floor of the building. He said he was asleep at the time of the explosion.

"I figured it was a building across the road from me and when I got up, I seen no window, a big hole in the wall. When I looked to my right, I seen the red flames and I said that's fire — I'm getting out," Marr told CBC News.
Marr said he had to crawl to get out of the building without his shoes. He said his right hand was cut and his body is sore. He said he lost everything, including his wallet and a safe with his will.
Marr said he's glad everybody made it out, but that he's in shock. He said he's worried about finding a new place to live because winter is coming.

articles.title: Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have held trilateral talks ― but what did they achieve?
articles.summary: The presidents of China, the US and Russia have held an unprecedented summit. While Trump said the three leaders were "making history," Xi described the talks as "fruitful" and Putin called them…

image.caption: The 'peace declaration' released after their meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the US-led war in IranImage: Doug Mills/The New York Times/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday for an unprecedented trilateral summit in Shenzhen, bringing together the leaders of the world's three most powerful military powers amid heightened geopolitical tensions.
Xi hailed the talks as "groundbreaking," saying discussions ranged from global governance and denuclearization to the war in Ukraine and energy security.
The "peace declaration" released after their meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the US-led war in Iran.

Instead, the three leaders agreed to pursue reforms of the United Nations, limit the role of the International Criminal Court and reaffirm their commitment to avoiding nuclear war. They also pledged to boost supplies of refined petroleum products to address global energy challenges.
The tightly choreographed meeting fueled concerns that Beijing, Washington and Moscow could seek to reshape the international order around competing spheres of influence.
While Xi said the talks with Trump and Putin were "positive, constructive and fruitful," Trump heralded the gathering as "really making history."
Leaders of China, Russia, US praise trilateral summit as 'success'
Who gained the most from the meeting?

For Putin, the three-way talks, and his meetings with both leaders separately earlier, offered a chance to show the world that he was on par with the leaders of the US and China, despite Western efforts to isolate him since he launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Emma Chanlett-Avery, senior director for Political-Security Affairs at the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI), said Putin had the most to gain from the meeting as "he appeared on the world stage as one of the dominant players in the world."
Chim Lee, a senior analyst with The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU), echoed this view.
The meeting itself is a "major outcome for Russia," he told DW, pointing to Russian media coverage that has cast it as "reinforcing Russia's standing in the world."
Beijing reluctant to accept nuclear limits
The joint statement also said the leaders are committed to work to reduce nuclear risks and prevent nuclear proliferation.
The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, known as New START, expired in February.
Trump has said he wants "a new, improved and modernized" deal that includes China.
But Beijing has so far been reluctant to accept limits as its estimated arsenal of around 500 warheads remains far smaller than those of Russia and the US.
Moscow and Washington are believed to possess more than 5,000 warheads each.
Why China is surging its nuclear forces
Lee said China is unlikely to participate in a trilateral institutionalized setting to control nuclear arms.

"The gap between China's nuclear arsenal and those of Russia and US is still quite large. From China's perspective, it doesn't seem to make a lot of sense to put the three powers in the same bucket in this area."
The expert believes Trump attended the meeting as he is "actively thinking about his legacy in the final two years in office."
"So, in this context, the idea of setting up a trilateral nuclear arms control arrangement would have been a very big achievement," Lee said.
But, in the end, the declaration said the countries would merely engage in "dialogue" on the issue, avoiding any explicit commitments to downsize their nuclear stockpiles.
A reluctant host?

China initially hesitated to organize the trilateral summit as it did not want to be explicitly tied to Russia's war in Ukraine and harm Beijing's efforts to present itself as a long-term force for global stability.
The Chinese government, which is working to rebalance economic ties with the EU, was also wary of appearing to form a G3 club with Washington and Moscow, which could alienate other global partners.
Chanlett-Avery said that China had some degree of discomfort in convening this meeting, worried about getting involved in Ukraine issues.
But Beijing eventually "managed to get the outcome they wanted" and kept the European conflict out of the meeting's focus, she noted.

"China was able to show off Shenzhen and all of its sparkling high-tech features. They convened a successful international meeting that grabbed lots of headlines," she added. "So, I think China probably came out feeling okay."
Warnings of a 'second Yalta'
Prior to the summit, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned of a "second Yalta," referring to the Yalta Conference held in Crimea in 1945.
That meeting saw the Allied powers decide on the post-war European order following the end of World War II.

In Shenzhen, Putin stressed that Russia, the US and China, as victors in World War II and veto-wielding members of the UN Security Council, bore a "joint responsibility for maintaining international peace."

But Ying-Yu Lin, Associate Professor at Graduate Institute of International Affairs and Strategic Studies at Taiwan's Tamkang University, said the Yalta comparison "is a bit of a stretch," given the vast differences between 1945 and now.
Why Russia and China aren't really best friends
Will there be more such trilaterals?
Putin also said that all three leaders "agree that it's a useful format," and such meetings could take place again.
Lee, the EIU expert, said the trilateral setup "is unlikely to be just a one-off" and there will probably be more such meetings in the coming years.
"Especially from the US side to have this kind of setup, there will be some interest in maintaining warm relations with both China and Russia," he underlined.

articles.title: Myanmar ruling gives new relevance to genocide convention and is ‘full of messages’ for Israel
articles.summary:
Hailed as ‘a rare moment of justice’, judges’ decision sets out a roadmap for assessing the question of intent

The

blocks.text: The international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims. It also gives the 1948 genocide convention new relevance in governing the actions of nation states.

In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused of committing genocide against a whole population group, especially when it comes to assessing the question of intent.
The lengthy judgment will have been read particularly carefully by Israel, the only other country currently before the ICJ accused of genocide.
It is also relevant to Germany, which has been brought before the court by Nicaragua on the accusation it has facilitated and failed to prevent genocide in Gaza.

“I think it’s a judgment that brings the genocide convention alive,” said Philippe Sands, a leading human rights lawyer who was part of the Gambian legal team. “It gives the convention practical, real meaning. And if the alternative view had been taken, the convention would essentially become a dead letter.”

Amnesty International’s secretary general, Agnès Callamard, called the ruling “a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families”. But it was also an assertion of humanitarian law in an increasingly lawless world.

“This is a good day for international law. We needed it,” said Dr Iva Vukušić, an assistant professor in international History at Utrecht University and a war crimes expert. “It is really important, clarifying a lot of law, and that’s going to be very helpful going forward.”

There will be a spillover from this ruling to its sister tribunal in The Hague, the international criminal court (ICC), providing a benchmark for when genocide charges could be made against individual perpetrators.

The Trump administration, instinctively hostile to international legal institutions, is also watching critically. The US ambassador to the UN told the ICJ before this judgment not to “lower the legal threshold for proving genocide” lest it be “weaponised” against US and allied soldiers.
The court did not directly lower the standard for demonstrating genocide, and the Gambia – which brought the case to The Hague – did not ask it to.

The judges kept the existing benchmark for judging genocide intent as the “only reasonable inference” of Myanmar’s actions and referred extensively to prior case law. But it went a long way towards clarifying how that standard should be applied in assessing atrocity crimes committed by states.

Before this case, only Serbia had faced the charge of genocide at the ICJ, in cases brought by Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the Bosnian ruling in 2007, Belgrade was found to have failed to prevent the 1995 genocide in Srebrenica, but in both cases it was cleared of committing the genocide directly.

The new ICJ judgment finds the Myanmar military directly responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, a Muslim minority targeted in a ferocious counterinsurgency campaign that reached its peak in 2017.

In assessing the Myanmar campaign, the ICJ looked not just at the death toll of about 10,000 in assessing the scale of the atrocities, but at the total Rohingya population targeted in northern Rakhine state, 815,000 people. Significantly, it cast its net wider than just the death toll, considering mental damage done to the survivors, particularly victims of sexual violence, and the impact on reproduction in the Rohingya community.

Most importantly, the ICJ judgment provided a guide to interpreting the standard set by Serbian cases, in which a finding of genocide could be made only if there were not other plausible motives for mass killing.

In this judgment, the court ruled that Myanmar could have had other motives, such as the desire to displace or punish the Rohingya population, but that those motives could exist alongside genocidal intent. The judges said genocidal intent was the “only reasonable inference” from the “totality” of evidence.

In justifying that conclusion the judges pointed to several factors that international law experts say are relevant to the Gaza case, which is now hearing written pleadings and is expected to take at least another three years.

The common factors include the targeting of children, which the court described as striking at the “foundation” of the Rohingya as a group – the ICJ said up to 2,109 Rohingya children under the age of five had been killed, while more than 5,000 Palestinian children under five years old have been killed in the Gaza war.

Another incriminating factor cited by the court was the “bulldozing and large-scale terrain clearance” after the destruction of villages, followed by “rapid construction” including security installations, which has been the hallmark of Israeli army occupation of over 60% of the Gaza Strip.

“It’s full of messages for Israel,” said William Schabas, an international law professor and expert on genocide at Middlesex University. “There are obvious differences, of course, the evidence will be different, but if you exchanged the word Myanmar with Israel, you wouldn’t have to change much in the judgment.”

The fact that there were six dissenting voices on the bench suggested that substantial parts of the majority’s reasoning were not beyond dispute, and lawyers involved in the case cautioned that it did not necessarily mean that the same bench would find Israel guilty of genocide in Gaza. But the same lawyers added that the opposite was almost certainly true. If this case had failed, the case brought by South Africa against Israel would have been all but over.

articles.title: Duterte's defense witness admits Cale88 has 'red flags'
articles.summary: A defense witness in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte admitted that there were "red flags" in the operations of Cale88 but said these do not necessarily mean wrongdoing.

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 1:12am

A witness for the defense in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte admitted that there were "red flags" in the operations of Cale88, but maintained that these do not necessarily mean wrongdoing.

Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros asked AML Consulting PH head Rainer Dela Fuente whether he knew if Cale88—the food company being linked to Duterte's spouse Manases Carpio—had a legitimate explanation for its suspicious transactions reports to the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC).
Dela Fuente replied in the negative.
“Masasabi niyo po bang unusual itong total of 757 CTRs and STRs na may halagang P1,245,736,297.8?” Hontiveros asked.
(Would you say that having 757 covered transaction reports [CTRs] and suspicious transaction reports [STRs] worth P1,245,736,297.8 is unusual?)
Dela Fuente said that only the AMLC could determine if this was suspicious, but maintained that suspicion is not a direct indication of unlawful activity.
He said that there are with many more CTRs and STRs than what Cale88 had.
Hontiveros asked about the AMLC's flagging Cale88’s two employees, as well as its transactions with China.
"Lastly po, Attorney De La Fuente, hindi po ba yan posibleng mga [are these not possible] red flags?" Hontiveros asked.
"Yes, these are red flags po that merit…scrutiny, review, opo, but again red flags po are not direct evidence of wrongdoing, " Dela Fuente replied.

During Hontiveros’ questioning, Dela Fuente also said that he previously worked with gambling businesses and Philippine Offshore Gaming Operators. He was also a previous consultant for the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation (PAGCOR). — BM, GMA News
