articles.title: No mention of fossil fuels in latest COP31 draft deal
articles.summary: One of the most fraught debates at the UN climate talks in Turkey has revolved around the future of coal, oil and gas. Now all mention of fossil fuels has been removed from the summit's new draft…

image.caption: Protestors at the COP31 in Antalya Turkey calling for a phaseout of fossil fuels, the burning of which is the main driver of climate changeImage: DW

blocks.text: Climate negotiators have removed any mention of fossil fuels — the main source of greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet — in a new draft deal published by COP31 summit co-host Australia.

The latest text released Thursday at the UN climate conference in Turkey stripped out two references to a transition away from coal, oil and gas and a call for an accelerated phaseout that had been in an earlier draft.
This slimmed down version follows days of tough negotiations with representatives from nearly 200 countries on issues such as the future of fossil fuels and climate funding for developing countries.
The text also includes a call to increase the global share of final energy demand met by electricity to 35% by 2035 — up from around 20% today — a proposal that had been pushed by host Turkey.

blocks.caption: COP31 negotiators are once again gearing up to fight to have fossil fuels mentioned in a final decision in the yearly UN climate summitImage: Dilara Senkaya/REUTERS

blocks.text: It did not specify whether that additional electricity needs to come from clean sources, a point that has drawn criticism from some countries. But it did link the target to efforts to triple renewable energy capacity globally alongside other energy efficiency measures.
What else is in the draft text?

The draft text also expressed "deep concern" that global warming is projected to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels — the threshold outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avoid runaway climate change.
It acknowledged that every increment of warming above current levels would "result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems."

It also recognized the need for "deep, rapid ​and ‌sustained" cuts to greenhouse gas emissions and called for efforts to ramp up action targeting the potent greenhouse gas methane. The greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet are largely caused by burning fossil fuels.
COP31: Can electrification replace fossil fuels?
The text additionally calls for the deployment of technologies that can remove carbon from the atmosphere to be sped up — those technologies are as yet largely unproven at scale.

Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign to boost climate finance for developing countries said the second draft "trims away inconvenient mandates and accountability while leaving behind lofty rhetoric that won't protect a single vulnerable community."

"It is actively more regressive, stripping out hard-won accountability, timelines, and legal anchors just as frontline communities in the Global South are paying the steepest price for climate breakdown," said Singh in a statement.
Talks in crunch time
The climate conference officially ends on Friday, but it's not uncommon for the annual talks to run overtime. The latest text is expected to face further revisions before it can be adopted.
Decisions on the language need approval from all countries, meaning an objection from one party is enough to scupper a deal.
On Thursday, Panama said it would block any agreement that does not meet its demand for a cap on oil production and steps to eliminate the potent greenhouse gas methane.
The country's environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, said Panama "not lend its name" to "complacent or ineffective language" in the final pact.

blocks.caption: A glacier collapse linked to planetary heating killed thousands in Nepal in AugustImage: Francis Mascarenhas/REUTERS

blocks.text: The stakes are high for this edition of the COP summit, which comes in a year of major climate-related disasters, from wildfires and deadly heat waves in Europe to a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people.
It's also taking place against the backdrop of an intensifying "super" El Nino weather pattern, and geopolitical shocks that have sent energy prices rising globally.

It's the first conference taking place with the acknowledgement by the UN that keeping the average global temperature under 1.5C is no longer realistic. Instead, scientists are talking about limiting the time spent above this threshold and bringing temperatures back down rapidly by the end of the century.
More to come…

articles.title: Venezuela signs military deal with US less than a year after Maduro's ouster
articles.summary: The US Secretary of Defence says Venezuela has 'gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner'.

blocks.text: The United States and Venezuela have re-established military ties less than a year after US forces seized the then-leader of the South American country, Nicolás Maduro, in a raid on the capital, Caracas.
The interim government led by Delcy Rodríguez, Maduro's former vice-president, signed a military co-operation agreement with US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth on Wednesday.
Few details about the deal have been released so far but Hegseth said that Venezuela had "gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner" in less than 12 months.
Interim President Rodríguez said the deal would help confront "common threats".
Military co-operation between the two countries was terminated in 2005 by Hugo Chávez, Venezuela's left-wing president at the time.
Chávez alleged that US military personnel sent to Venezuela to train their counterparts had made disparaging remarks about his government.
He also accused the US military office located in Fuerte Tiuna, Venezuela's largest military complex, of being "an organ of the CIA... conspiring against the government".
Under Nicolás Maduro, who succeeded Chávez after the latter's death from cancer, relations between the two countries deteriorated further.
They reached rock bottom late last year when the US doubled its reward for information leading to Maduro's capture to $50m (£38m) and eventually seized him on 3 January in a military raid.
Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, are now in custody in New York on charges of drug-trafficking and conspiracy to commit torture, which they deny.
Hegseth addressed the change in the two countries' relationship since Maduro was seized in his speech at the US embassy in Caracas on Wednesday.
"It's a great honour to be here as the first United States Secretary of War this century to set foot in Venezuela. The weight of this moment does not escape me," he said.

"Just one year ago, my presence here, our presence here would have been deemed impossible, almost unimaginable," he added before recalling a public appearance by then-President Maduro which had angered the Trump administration.

"Exactly one year ago today, the indicted narco-terrorist fugitive Nicolás Maduro, the man who spent more than a decade handing Venezuela's borders and territory to terrorists from all over the world, stood on a stage, not too far from here, and yelled mockingly: 'Come and get me!'. Well, we answered that call."
Hegseth added that the result of the US military raid on 3 January had been as Maduro predicted, quoting the deposed leader's words: "No war, yes peace."

He described the deal signed by him and Venezuela's defence minister on Wednesday as a "new chapter for the United States, for Venezuela, for the Venezuelan military and for the Western Hemisphere through the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition".
Rodríguez described it as "extraordinarily relevant for our bilateral relations".

"In a matter of months, secretary, we have turned very difficult moments for our people into a space for co-operation and mutual benefit for both of our countries," she said addressing Hegseth during a meeting at the presidential palace.

While no details of the deal have been published, in her speech Rodríguez mentioned the training of Venezuela's armed forces and improving its "operational equipment" and access to new technology "to confront shared threats".

In his speech at the US embassy, Hegseth was more direct about who he considers to be those threats. Addressing "the narco-terrorists who abuse this [Venezuela] as a safe haven", he warned that "we will hunt you down, we will find you, and we will kill you".
From Venezuela, Hegseth travelled on to neighbouring Colombia, whose president, Abelardo de la Espriella, is a close ally of the Trump administration.
Colombia is already part of the US-led Americas Counter Cartel Coalition and in August, Hegseth had floated the possibility of joint US-Colombian military operations against armed groups.
On Wednesday, President de la Espriella took to X to deny a report by the New York Times which had stated that he had rejected carrying out joint operations, external.
In his post, he stressed that any decision would be taken while respecting Colombia's constitution, and the country's laws and sovereignty.
Hegseth reposted the tweet commenting that the US-Colombian partnership "is stronger than ever before".

articles.title: Pakistan minister to visit India, but no breakthrough expected
articles.summary: A Pakistani minister's visit to India for a Shanghai Cooperation Organization forum marks a rare high-level contact between the two archrivals, but analysts say it does not signal a resumption of…

image.caption: It's the first India visit by a Pakistani federal minister since the two neighbors fought a four-day conflict last yearImage: Aman Sharma/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Pakistan's Climate Change Minister Musadik Masood Malik will travel to India from November 20 to 22 to participate in the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Civilizational Dialogue in New Delhi.
It marks the first India visit by a Pakistani federal minister since the two nuclear-armed archrivals fought a four-day war last year.

The fighting erupted after armed gunmen killed over two dozen tourists, mostly Hindus, in India-administered Kashmir in April 2025. New Delhi accused Islamabad of backing the attack, a charge Pakistan denied.
Since the military confrontation, diplomatic tensions have remained high, leaving little room for official engagement between the two sides.
The SCO Civilizational Dialogue was proposed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the SCO summit in Tianjin in September 2025.
As the forum's host, India has invited all member states to participate in the event.
The SCO is a political, economic, and security alliance established in 2001. Belarus, China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan are its current members.

blocks.caption: Pakistan's Climate Change Minister Musadik Masood Malik will participate in the Shanghai Cooperation Organization Civilizational Dialogue in New DelhiImage: Dogukan Keskinkilic/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: A 'good sign'

Ajay Bisaria, a former Indian ambassador to Pakistan, sees significance in the fact that neither side sought to avoid the engagement. "The real takeaway is that the relationship isn't so broken that India won't invite Pakistan, or that Pakistan won't come. That alone is a good sign," he told DW.
But Bisaria cautions against assuming that the invitation followed a diplomatic breakthrough.

"The trigger was procedural. This forum grew out of Modi's proposal at the 2025 SCO summit in Tianjin, and as host, New Delhi invited every SCO member. I see no evidence of a back channel or outside mediation, and I wouldn't read much into that either way," he said.
'Being pragmatic'
The multilateral setting serves both countries, though for different reasons.

Pakistan wants to retain its influence within the organization. It currently holds the chairmanship of the SCO Council of Heads of State for 2026–27 and is due to host the next leaders' summit in Islamabad in August 2027.

Ayesha Siddiqa, a Pakistani expert on military and security affairs at King's College London, argues that Islamabad's decision to send a senior minister should be understood primarily in terms of its position in the grouping.

"Pakistan is keen to maintain its position and influence within the SCO and does not want to relinquish its role in the organization. The minister's visit should therefore be seen primarily in the context of Pakistan fulfilling its commitments under the SCO Charter, rather than as a gesture towards India," Siddiqa told DW.
A 'frozen conflict': India-Pakistan tensions persist
T C A Raghavan, another former Indian ambassador to Pakistan, shares a similar sentiment.

"Both India and Pakistan attach importance to the SCO, and Pakistan currently holds its chairmanship. This visit should be seen primarily in the context of the SCO, rather than as a development in India-Pakistan bilateral relations," Raghavan told DW.

"Islamabad is also being pragmatic in keeping channels open during its SCO chairmanship by participating in an initiative championed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. There will be no real impact on the India-Pakistan bilateral."
The bilateral freeze
Since the April 2025 attack, India has maintained that terrorism and talks cannot go hand in hand.

"Post the Pahalgam attack, we have a Pakistan policy. That Pakistan policy remains in place. There has been no change," Randhir Jaiswal, spokesperson for India's Foreign Ministry, said at the end of October.
Pakistan, meanwhile, continues to raise the issues of Kashmir and the Indus Waters Treaty, which New Delhi placed "in abeyance" following the attack.

Malik, the climate change minister traveling to India, has been a prominent voice in Pakistan's campaign over water rights. In June, he warned: "We will protect ourselves... if anyone lays a hand over our share of water, we'll cut off that hand."
Sanjay Kumar Bhardwaj, professor at the Center for South Asian Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University, said the SCO is part of India's "multi-aligned foreign policy."
He noted that the forum "doesn't provide any space to normalize relations with Pakistan."

blocks.caption: The SCO Civilizational Dialogue was proposed by Prime Minister Narendra ModiImage: Pyotr Kovalev/Sputnik/Kremlin Pool Photo/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Unofficial channels, no formal dialogue
The absence of official talks, however, does not mean all bilateral communication has stopped.

Since the May 2025 confrontation, Indian and Pakistani former diplomats, strategic experts, parliamentarians and retired military officers have reportedly taken part in a series of informal or semi-official back-channel meetings.
Such exchanges allow participants to assess the other side's thinking, keep informal lines of communication open and reduce the risk of miscalculation.
But they do not amount to formal negotiations. New Delhi has said retired officials attending such meetings do so in their personal capacities.

An assessment by the International Institute for Strategic Studies in November said both governments appeared reluctant to resume secret talks, despite the role earlier back-channel contacts had played in stabilizing relations.
Bisaria described the visit by a Pakistani minister to India as "a modest step forward, not a breakthrough."
What happens next, he said, "depends on Pakistan."

"If it avoids grandstanding in Delhi and offers credible assurances on terrorism, publicly or quietly, it becomes more likely that Indian leaders will attend next year's SCO summit in Islamabad. That will be the real test."

articles.title: Defense witness grilled over ‘useless’ testimony
articles.summary: Lawyer Rainer Dela Fuente cites confidentiality to explain why he did not review prosecution witness Alex Cabrera's forensic report, prompting criticisms from several senator-judges

blocks.text: EXPERT. Defense witness Rainer Dela Fuente testifies on Day 44 of Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial on November 19, 2026.
Lawyer Rainer Dela Fuente cites confidentiality to explain why he did not review prosecution witness Alex Cabrera's forensic report, prompting criticisms from several senator-judges

items: Defense witness Rainer Dela Fuente admitted he had not read the prosecution's financial forensic report or its supporting documents before testifying in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Dela Fuente's lack of review raised concerns among senator-judges about the validity of his testimony, with some questioning how he could refute the report's findings without having seen the underlying documents.

The prosecution challenged Dela Fuente's qualifications and expertise, emphasizing the importance of context in evaluating financial reports, particularly in light of allegations of unexplained wealth against Duterte.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – A defense witness admitted that he had not read the prosecution’s financial forensic report or reviewed its supporting documents before testifying in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Thursday, November 19.
Lawyer Rainer Dela Fuente, a former Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) financial investigator, was presented as an expert witness for the defense on Day 44 of the trial.
During his direct examination, defense lawyer Mark Vinluan sought to challenge the methodology and findings of the financial forensic report prepared by prosecution witness Alex Cabrera.

blocks.caption: Financial analyst tells impeach court: Sara Duterte has P817M in undisclosed wealth

blocks.text: Dela Fuente, however, told the impeachment court that he had not been provided copies of the report and its supporting documents before the hearing.

“No, Your Honor,” Dela Fuente said when asked whether he had received copies of AMLC records, bank statements, insurance placements, and general information sheets (GIS) of companies linked to Duterte.
Vinluan confirmed that the witness had not reviewed the entire report, saying the defense intended to focus on specific portions of the 50-page document.
“If he is to refute the report, then he should have seen the report, should have read the report,” Senator-judge Joel Villanueva said.
“Now if he cannot answer these questions then, for me, it’s going to be useless,” Villanueva added.
Other senator-judges, including Erwin Tulfo, also questioned how Dela Fuente could examine the report’s findings without reviewing the underlying documents.

“Kung hindi naman niya po nakita pala ay mga dokumento, STRs (Suspicious Transaction Reports), CTRs (Covered Transaction Reports), what good is it? Para anong tetestigo niya, eh puro ito theory sa kanyang paningin, sa kanyang paniniwala,” Tulfo said.
(If has has not seen the documents, STRs, CTRs, what good is it? What’s his testimony for, it’ll just be all his theory, his beliefs.)
He added: “The witnesses you’ve been presenting here these past few days are weak. Get somebody who can really stand up, who can really answer questions from the senator-judges.”
Dela Fuente was listed as a defense witness who would testify on fundamental legal concepts under the Anti-Money Laundering Act (AMLA).

Explaining why he did not review the report and its supporting documents, Dela Fuente cited confidentiality concerns. He also said he was not dismissing Cabrera’s findings but was merely answering the defense’s hypothetical questions based on his understanding of the law.

“Ang akin lang pong saligan ay ang ating AMLA, ang ating batas, so I can answer based on the law… Ako personally, ayoko basahin yung report because coming here, and wala rin ako access sa report, coming here and reading that report, I will develop biases,” Dela Fuente said.

(My only basis is our AMLA, and our laws, so I can answer based on the law… Personally, I don’t want to read the report because coming here, and I also did not have access to the report, coming here here and reading that report, I will develop biases.)
The prosecution tried to paint Dela Fuente as unqualified.

“Your claimed expertise as a financial expert in financial investigation only comes from the 25 months that you were an entry-level investigator for the AMLC. Is that correct?” Diokno asked Dela Fuente, who answered in the affirmative.

Dela Fuente also admitted that he was not challenging the accuracy or truthfulness of the AMLC reports, Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) records, and bank records involving the Vice President.
Diokno, like the senators, also made a big deal of the fact that Dela Fuente did not read the forensic examination report prepared by the prosecution’s witness, Alexander Cabrera.

“Let’s say that I were going to evaluate your investigation report,” Diokno said. “If in my evaluation, I decide not to read everything and pick portions only, don’t you think it will be unfair to you?”
“You didn’t read the whole report. Wouldn’t you agree that context means a lot in terms of evaluating the veracity of a financial report?” Diokno added.

Cabrera previously testified that based on his analysis of the Vice President’s bank and financial records, Duterte, and her husband, Mans Carpio, had accumulated P817 million unexplained wealth from 2022 to 2025.
Duterte is being tried for Article II of the Articles of Impeachment, which involves allegations of unexplained wealth. – with reports from Dwight de Leon/Rappler.com

articles.title: What is a stake at the EU-UK summit in Brussels?
articles.summary: Leaders will wrestle with easing Brexit red tape, restoring emissions trading and opening up youth mobility

blocks.text: The EU and UK will hold a long-awaited summit in Brussels on Friday – the second since Brexit – to hammer out the UK’s longer-term relationship with the bloc.
It will be attended by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and the president of the European Council, António Costa.
The gathering, which follows up last year’s inaugural EU-UK summit in London, was scheduled for July but postponed when Keir Starmer resigned.

blocks.caption: EU negotiators want their students to pay tuition fees at UK levels instead of the much higher international rate. Photograph: Chris Ison/PA

blocks.text: What is on the table?
The two sides hope to announce three deals, which were launched under Starmer’s government.

First, a food and drink agreement that will remove a lot of Brexit red tape on animal and plant products, making it easier to trade meats, cheese, wine and flowers. To secure the deal, which is not expected to take effect until 2028, the UK will align with EU standards, meaning the government, for example, must abandon a planned ban on foie gras imports.

A second agreement will link the British emissions trading system with its bigger EU cousin, restoring a link severed by Brexit. It is a significant step for industry because EU and UK businesses will be exempt from each other’s charges on high-carbon imports such as steel, cement and electricity. This agreement also requires alignment with relevant EU rules.

The third deal is the most contentious: a youth mobility scheme that will give 18- to 30-year-olds the right to live, work, travel and study on both sides of the Channel for up to three years. The scheme may not be up and running until 2030 – bad news for anyone in their late 20s.

With less than 24 hours before the summit begins, two big issues remain open. EU negotiators want to ensure EU students pay the UK rate of university tuition, around four or five times lower than international fees. The two sides also disagree over how many people would be allowed to take part: the EU wants 100,000 visas a year, but the UK is looking at 50,000 to 80,000 to keep migration numbers down.
To maximise its leverage on tuition fees, the EU is linking the three agreements, warning they must enter force together.
Will the UK be included in Made in Europe?

Not on Friday. The UK has been pushing for inclusion in the EU’s Made in Europe plan, a protectionist scheme to favour EU companies when public money is being spent on goods such as electric cars, renewable energy and nuclear technology. Inclusion in Made in Europe is a big priority for the Burnham government, which has dangled major concessions on tuition fees to make sure British firms are not shut out.

The problem for London is that the EU lawmakers have not finalised the Made in Europe law, known as the Industrial Accelerator Act. Many EU member states want to include the UK, but France and the European parliament take a stricter position.

The EU law is not expected to be agreed until spring 2027. To help the British government, which has linked a generous offer on youth mobility with Made in Europe, the European Commission proposed delaying agreement on tuition fees by six months. But member states want precise guarantees now about equal treatment for EU students.

Another problem is that British inclusion in Made in Europe requires the UK to sign up to EU trade-defence policies. The EU, for instance, has imposed high tariffs on “unfairly subsidised” Chinese electric cars and fears the UK, which has not followed suit, could become an alternative route into the EU if Chinese companies set up in Britain and sell into the bloc. The EU is calling on the UK to align with its trade-defence policies, but the UK insists it can guard against circumvention without copying the EU.
In a sign of possible tensions, an earlier summit text proposing a trusted partnership on economic security has been downgraded to a partnership.

blocks.caption: An agreement expected next year will bring the UK back into the EU’s internal electricity market. Photograph: CW Images/Alamy

blocks.text: What happens next?

Beyond the headline deals, the EU-UK draft summit statement opens the door to British integration in European policies on energy, crime-fighting, educational exchange, tech and foreign policy cooperation.

The next major agreement, targeted for next year, is bringing the UK back into the EU’s internal electricity market. This is a priority for five EU member states – Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark and Luxembourg. They argue that Britain’s inclusion in the EU electricity market is essential to take advantage of the nascent green power boom in the North Sea. In return for market access, the UK will be required to contribute to the EU budget to aid the development of poorer EU regions.
Beyond that, the two sides will “explore opportunities” for the UK to join the Erasmus student exchange programme after 2027 – the current arrangement applies only for the 2027/8 academic year.

In a win for the UK, the EU appears ready to expand talks on the mutual recognition of professional qualifications, beyond existing negotiations on architects. The sides will sign a digital partnership, which includes joint work on AI safety. And examine how to share data on law enforcement and border management.
Is this joining the EU by the backdoor?

Far from it. A lot of diplomatic plates are spinning, but the UK remains outside the EU’s biggest economic clubs: the single market and the customs union. It also has no decision-making powers inside the EU.

Burnham says he will set out the long-term options for the future relationship after this week’s summit. “The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain,” he said on Monday in a major speech. But amid concerns among some cabinet ministers about reopening Brexit divides, the prime minister appears to be taking a more cautious approach. He said the process would take time and insisted that “at every stage the British people will be the boss”.
The EU has welcomed Britain’s interest in rejoining but is wary of a protracted negotiation that could be reversed by an anti-EU British government.
In an echo of the Brexit years, EU insiders say, once again, that it is up to Britain to define what it wants.

image.caption: Putin, Xi and Trump have met for highly anticipated trilateral talksImage: Win McNamee/REUTERS

blocks.text: November 19, 2026
What do we know about agreements at the trilateral summit?
The highly anticipated three-way talks between US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday have ended.
Ahead of the talks, Trump said they would be about "all problems that are being discussed in the world"
Here are quotes from the leaders and from a joint statement on the topics they addressed:
Nuclear arms

items: Trump: "The United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lessen the risk of those weapons being used."

Xi: "A nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. Every effort must be made to prevent nuclear war, adhere to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, and maintain global strategic stability."

blocks.text: International Criminal Court and UN

items: In a joint statement reported by Chinese state media and the Kremlin, the leaders agreed that "the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction."
The leaders also "acknowledged the vital importance of the principle of state consent and the respect for (diplomatic) immunity enjoyed by state officials."
The statement added that all three countries were "committed" to advancing reform of the United Nations.

blocks.text: Energy

items: The joint statement said the countries "plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products."
It reaffirmed "the importance of the stable flow of energy."

blocks.text: Neither the war in Ukraine nor the conflict in Iran were directly mentioned at the talks, according to the Russian and Chinese accounts.

articles.title: US consortium wins huge Kenya mining deal, beating Chinese rivals
articles.summary: The Mrima Hill site is estimated to hold deposits of critical minerals worth more than $60bn (£45bn).

blocks.text: A US-led consortium, Frontier Minerals, has won the tender to develop Kenya's Mrima Hill mining project, beating seven bidders, including companies from China and Australia.
The site is estimated to hold deposits of critical minerals worth more than $60bn (£45bn), including niobium, used in electric vehicles, aerospace and defence technology.
Frontier Minerals says its proposal aims to keep more of the economic benefits in Kenya through "processing and refining of minerals in-country".
The deal comes as Washington seeks greater access to Africa's minerals, aiming to strengthen US supply chains and compete with China.

Frontier Minerals brings together three US companies - Bunker Hill Mining Corp, American Resources Corporation and ReElement Technologies Corporation. The consortium combines expertise in mineral resource development, critical materials supply chains and advanced refining technologies.

A central part of its proposal is to develop mineral processing and refining capacity in Kenya. Brad Marnett from Frontier Minerals said the company wanted the country to capture more value from its mineral resources.
Mrima Hill is located in Kwale County, near Kenya's Indian Ocean coastline. The site covers about 390 acres of forest.
The prospect of mining in the area has raised concerns among local residents, who fear the project could damage the forest and threaten their ancestral heritage.
There are also questions over whether communities living near the site will benefit from the investment.

Marnett was keen to reassure Kenyans that they would benefit: "We intend to create lasting opportunities for Kenyan workers, businesses and the wider economy through capacity-building and targeted investment, while prioritising environmental management and performance."
The consortium must still obtain a prospecting licence and meet the necessary regulatory requirements before the project can proceed.
The tender decision has drawn objections from competing bidders.
Reuters news agency reports that two rival companies intend to challenge the selection, with Australia's RareX alleging that Frontier Minerals missed an earlier submission deadline.
Kenya's government has maintained that the process was open and transparent.
The project comes as US strives to secure alternative sources of critical minerals and reduce dependence on China, which dominates the processing of several key minerals.

Washington has been pursuing partnerships with mineral-rich African countries, including the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia, as it seeks to strengthen supply chains for industries ranging from electric vehicles to defence technology.
Kenya's mining ministry says the sector is an important part of its plans to diversify the economy beyond traditional sources of revenue such as tourism, agriculture and financial services.

articles.title: Car rams into Palestinian residents four times in Israeli city, injuring eight
articles.summary:
Arab MPs accuse Israeli politicians of fuelling hostility as footage shows driver accelerating towards pedestrians at several locations in Kafr Qasim

Eight people were injured on Wednesday…

blocks.text: Eight people were injured on Wednesday evening when a driver struck Palestinian residents at four separate locations in Kafr Qasim, a city in central Israel.

Footage shared on social media appears to show the car accelerating towards people, all Palestinians, at several locations in the city, striking them before driving away. Three of those injured were in moderate condition, and several of the victims were women leaving a nearby wedding, the Times of Israel reported.

Haaretz has reported that investigators are examining whether the driver struck people deliberately. Avi Levy, a police district commander, said the incident appeared to be a hit-and-run and that the driver had tested positive for drugs. He said the Shin Bet security service was taking part in the investigation and added that “as of this moment, nothing is coming up. The suspect has no criminal record.”

The incident prompted Arab lawmakers and activists to accuse Israeli politicians of fuelling hostility towards Arab citizens. Benjamin Netanyahu has called Arab parties “terror supporters” and said partnering with them would put Israel’s security at risk. The parties won a record 19 seats in the Knesset in the country’s recent election.

Yousef Jabareen, the chair of the Joint List, said the incident “raises difficult questions about the claim that the driver lost control”. He said: “I’ve been warning for weeks that the incitement against Arab citizens will turn into assaults and even assassinations.”

blocks.caption: An election billboard in the predominantly-Arab city of Kafr Qasim in central Israel. Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Said Issa, a community activist in Kafr Qasim, described the incident as an “act of terror”.
“Someone who loses control of his vehicle might hit one or two vehicles, but not multiple people in several different places,” Issa said. “The attacker struck at four locations, one after the other.”

In a separate incident in the occupied West Bank, the Palestinian foreign ministry called on Monday for an Israeli settler to be held accountable after eight Palestinians were run over and injured in Tuqu, south-east of Bethlehem. Local sources told the Anadolu news agency that the driver first struck three young men, then returned and ran over five others who had gathered to help them.

articles.title: Dividing the Lopez empire: Who decides what a family business is worth?
articles.summary: The experiences of other business families suggest that a workable settlement requires more than a willingness to stop fighting

blocks.text: PART 1 | Why the Lopez cousins are breaking up — and what other feuding dynasties teach us

What months of fighting in boardrooms, shareholders’ meetings, and public statements could not accomplish, the buying and selling of shares may finally achieve: a separation of the Lopez family businesses.

Between August and November 2026, Eugenio “Gabby” Lopez III’s branch sold its 25.68% stake in apex parent Lopez Inc. to Ramon Ang for ₱11.56 billion and agreed to buy First Philippine Holdings’ (FPH) controlling stake in Rockwell Land for ₱15.92 billion. In between, cousin Federico “Piki” Lopez locked down the boards of Lopez Holdings and FPH, securing his grip on the group’s energy and industrial core. (Click on these links below for the author’s special reports on these developments:
Part 1 | The Lopez heirs who ran Rockwell but never controlled itPart 2 | Why Gabby Lopez wants Rockwell as ABS-CBN strugglesPart 3 | Why Piki Lopez is letting Rockwell go

The cousins appear to be finding a way to stop running the same businesses together. But separating a family business is not as simple as dividing an inheritance, especially when the family’s interests are held through layers of private and publicly listed companies with other shareholders, employees, creditors, and business partners whose interests cannot simply be divided among the cousins.

Who decides what each business is worth? Who approves the sale? What happens when the buyer and seller are connected to rival branches of the same family? And what protects shareholders who were never part of the quarrel?

In the first story of this series, we examined why business families fight and why some choose to stay together while others separate. The Lopezes are hardly the first to confront these questions. Other families have negotiated settlements, divided companies, bought out dissatisfied relatives, or found ways to continue working together. Their experiences offer lessons on how families can manage either choice without damaging the businesses they own.

One source of conflict in family businesses is that relatives often wear several hats at once. A person may be a grandson of the founder, a shareholder, a director, and an executive, but these positions do not give him the same authority. Being a member of the family does not automatically entitle him to run the company, just as owning shares does not necessarily give him the right to dictate daily operations. Problems arise when relatives begin treating their different roles as though they were interchangeable.

Family-business advisers Josh Baron and Rob Lachenauer explain these distinctions through their Four-Room Model. Imagine a family enterprise as a house with four rooms: the family room, the owners’ room, the boardroom, and the management room. The family discusses shared values, relationships, and what it wants to preserve for future generations. Shareholders exercise ownership rights, including electing directors. Directors oversee the company, approve major corporate decisions, and hold management accountable, while executives handle operations, employees, budgets, and the implementation of strategy.

The same relative may enter all four rooms, but his authority in one does not automatically extend to another. Family-business adviser Enrique Soriano discussed these overlapping responsibilities during a webinar we conducted in June, when the Lopez feud was already unfolding.

The Lopez dispute illustrates why these distinctions matter. Gabby’s branch exercised ownership rights through its stake in Lopez Inc., while Piki had spent decades managing and directing the group’s energy businesses. When the cousins disagreed about investments, valuations, and corporate direction, their disagreement became a contest over who had the authority to make those decisions.

By September, Piki had secured the chairmanship of Lopez Holdings and FPH, while his brother Benjamin “Jay” Lopez became president, chief operating officer, and chief finance officer of Lopez Holdings, taking over three positions previously held by longtime executive Salvador Tirona. Piki remained chairman and chief executive officer, placing the two brothers in the principal leadership positions of the listed holding company.

The significance went beyond replacing one executive with another. Lopez Holdings sits above FPH in the ownership structure, and the people leading it exercise considerable influence over the group’s investments and corporate direction. Tirona had been a senior professional executive for decades, while Jay was a member of the controlling family branch. His appointment brought operational and financial leadership at the holding company more directly into Piki’s family circle.
Winning control of a board may settle who has corporate authority to make certain decisions. It does not necessarily resolve what the different shareholders want from the business.

The Aboitiz family offers a useful contrast. I interviewed the late Jon Ramon Aboitiz in 2017 for a story about the Cebu-based conglomerate and how it had evolved through generations of owners and managers. When my profile of him was published in 2018, shortly after his death, the family had already established a constitution, a family council, rules governing who could enter the business, and a succession process that included preparing members of different family branches and generations for leadership.

These arrangements were part of a larger philosophy about managing family wealth. Jon Ramon recalled how his grandfather, Ramon Aboitiz, required young family members to learn the business from the ground up, sometimes literally cleaning toilets aboard the family’s ships. Relatives who wanted to become executives had to work and prove themselves. The family also learned to distinguish its attachment to one another from its attachment to a particular business.

blocks.caption: The author interviewing Jon Ramon Aboitiz in 2017. Lala Rimando

blocks.text: “One of the first things my grandfather imparted was: ‘Never fall in love with your business,’” Jon Ramon told me. The Aboitizes eventually sold their shipping business under well-known brands SuperFerry and SuperCat, which were once central to the family’s identity, as they redirected capital and management attention toward businesses, such as power, which they believed had better prospects. If it was the right time to sell, for the right reason and at the right price, the family should sell and move on. (READ: Q&A with Jon Ramon Aboitiz: ‘Never fall in love with your business’)

The Po family, whose businesses include Century Pacific Food, also developed formal arrangements to manage family participation. In a 2019 Esquire profile, I wrote about Nanette Medved-Po becoming the first chairperson of the Po Family Council, a position that gave her a role in the family’s governance distinct from the management of its operating companies.

The Aboitiz and Po experiences show how family governance can provide a place for relatives to discuss shared interests and expectations without requiring every disagreement to become a corporate dispute. A family council can help relatives who are not executives remain informed and involved, while a family constitution can establish values, expectations, and policies concerning succession, employment, and the stewardship of family wealth.

blocks.caption: Dividing the Lopez empire: Who decides what a family business is worth?

blocks.text: The Lopez family, however, never finalized a family constitution. Efforts were made while second generation Oscar Lopez was the family patriarch, and again after the third generation assumed leadership of the businesses. Neither effort produced a completed constitution before the cousins’ war erupted in 2026.

That is a significant distinction. The Lopezes had a long family history, established businesses, and experienced professional managers, but they did not have a finalized family constitution that could provide a common reference for the competing branches when disagreements over investments, control, and leadership intensified.

A constitution, however, would not necessarily have prevented the feud. Soriano has emphasized that a family constitution is not enough, because an agreement on shared values is different from a contract establishing enforceable rights. Families may also need shareholders’ agreements specifying how shares can be sold, how their value will be determined, whether relatives have the first opportunity to buy, and how disputes will be resolved.

The bitter dispute behind another familiar Philippine brand, Green Cross rubbing alcohol, offers a warning about relying on family trust without written agreements. Gonzalo Co It, who established the business in 1952, said he placed shares in the names of his parents and siblings when he incorporated the company, believing they were holding those shares for him. He later accused relatives of taking control and diluting his ownership, allegations that became the subject of a long-running court dispute. In a 2014 interview, Gonzalo said his mistake was failing to document the arrangements because he trusted his family.

His attempt at reconciliation brought another painful lesson. In 2011, Gonzalo withdrew his appeal before the Supreme Court, hoping to settle the dispute with his siblings. The reconciliation never materialized, and the withdrawal threatened to end his legal remedies. In October 2016, the Supreme Court allowed him to reinstate his petition, although it did not decide who owned the disputed shares. The case illustrates why families need more than goodwill when they negotiate ownership and settlement arrangements: even an agreement to stop fighting should specify what each side is giving up, what it will receive, and what happens if the promised reconciliation fails.

A family council can help relatives discuss disagreements. A code of conduct can establish boundaries on how they treat one another. A shareholders’ agreement can address what happens when they no longer want to remain business partners. None guarantees that relatives will agree, but the arrangements can establish rules before every proposed decision is interpreted as an attempt by one branch to outmaneuver another.
The best time to negotiate an exit is when nobody is yet trying to leave.

Some families settle their differences without dividing their businesses. Others decide that separation offers a better chance of preserving both the enterprises and whatever remains of their relationships.

In Singapore, the Kwek family’s February 2025 boardroom confrontation at City Developments Limited ended after trusted intermediaries helped broker a truce. Father Kwek Leng Beng and son Sherman Kwek retained their executive positions, while the two independent directors whose appointments had sparked the dispute stepped down. The Ortigas family, meanwhile, ended its dispute over OCLP Holdings through a 2014 compromise involving Ayala Land and SM Prime Holdings, preserving the property business while sharing influence with powerful outside investors.

India’s Ambani family chose to divide operating businesses, with mother Kokilaben mediating the 2005 settlement between brothers Mukesh and Anil. The Murdochs reached a different arrangement in September 2025, strengthening Lachlan Murdoch’s future voting control over Fox Corporation and News Corp while compensating three siblings who exited the relevant trust arrangements.

These families took different routes, but each had to confront the same practical questions: Who would control the business, what would each relative receive, who would finance the arrangement, and what would happen to the companies afterward?

The Lopezes appear to be pursuing several mechanisms at once. Gabby’s branch sold its ownership interest in the private holding company to Ang. ABS-CBN sought new investors and fresh capital. Piki secured leadership of the listed holding companies. And FPH approved a proposed sale that would move Rockwell Land from Piki’s corporate sphere to Gabby’s investment vehicle.
These are not interchangeable transactions, even if they are unfolding against the same family dispute.

When Crème sold its 25.68% stake in Lopez Inc., to Ramon Ang for about P11 billion, it was selling shares it owned in a private holding company. It was not directly selling the assets of First Gen, ABS-CBN, Rockwell Land, or every other company associated with the Lopez group. The proceeds went to the selling shareholder, Gabby and the other heirs of second generation Lopez siblings, not automatically to the companies beneath Lopez Inc.

blocks.caption: The secret to the Lopez family’s enduring control of ABS-CBN

blocks.text: The proposed Rockwell transaction is different because FPH, a publicly listed company, is selling its controlling interest in another listed company to an investment vehicle associated with Gabby. The November board approval covers FPH’s 90.74% interest in Rockwell, including common and voting preferred shares, for almost P16 billion. The proposed transaction remains subject to conditions and regulatory requirements, including a mandatory tender offer.

FPH disclosed that BDO Capital & Investment Corporation provided an independent valuation range of P2.47 to P3.09 per common share, with the agreed P3 price toward the upper end of that range. The valuation provides a basis for assessing the price, but it does not automatically settle every question about the transaction.

FPH stands to receive nearly P16 billion that it could deploy toward energy, infrastructure, and other investments. But it would also surrender control of Rockwell, a mature property business that has contributed earnings and diversification to the group. Crème would acquire control of the property developer but would have to finance the purchase and comply with the obligations that accompany control of a listed company.

The question is not simply whether the cousins agree that P15.92 billion is an acceptable price. It is whether the transaction is fair to FPH and its shareholders, including those who are not members of the Lopez family. That requires examining the valuation, the handling of potential conflicts of interest, the directors’ decision-making, and compliance with corporate and securities rules.

Rockwell’s minority shareholders have interests of their own. A change in control triggers tender-offer requirements intended to provide eligible shareholders an opportunity to sell under the applicable rules. These investors did not negotiate the family’s arrangements, and their rights cannot depend on whether the cousins are satisfied with the deal.

ABS-CBN presents another example. Its P6-billion equity plan was intended to raise capital for a company that had struggled financially since losing its broadcast franchise in 2020. Issuing additional shares reduces the percentage ownership of existing investors who do not participate proportionately. Their shares are not confiscated, but they own a smaller portion of the enlarged company. Among those affected was Batangas representative Leandro Leviste, whose investment and Mother’s Day gift to Senator Loren Legarda I examined in an earlier Rappler report.

blocks.caption: Leandro Leviste’s ABS-CBN stake is shrinking, and so is everyone else’s

blocks.text: The distinction matters. The Lopez Inc., transaction allowed a family shareholder to sell an investment. The ABS-CBN recapitalization sought to raise money for the company. The Rockwell transaction would transfer control of a subsidiary and provide cash to FPH. Treating all three as one family divorce obscures the separate corporate decisions and the interests of other shareholders.

There is another reason a corporate divorce cannot be judged only by whether the relatives are happier afterward. The Lopezes control companies with employees, executives, lenders, and shareholders who are not members of the family. These people did not start the dispute, but its consequences can affect their investments, careers, and livelihoods.

At an April townhall, Piki told First Gen employees there was no need to take sides in the family conflict. He urged them to continue doing their jobs professionally. ABS-CBN executives, meanwhile, were trying to keep employees focused on their work while the company’s financial difficulties and changes in ownership created uncertainty. The media company had already undergone repeated rounds of retrenchment since losing its broadcast franchise in 2020, and another program affected about 200 employees in September 2026. The layoffs cannot simply be attributed to the family feud, but the employees were confronting another period of uncertainty while the company’s owners and investors were making major decisions about its future.

blocks.caption: Why ABS-CBN is still retrenching 200 employees with P6 billion on the way

blocks.text: The dispute also unfolded alongside changes involving longtime executives Salvador Tirona and Enrique “Ike” Quiason, as well as independent directors Roberto Panlilio and Consuelo Garcia of Lopez Holdings. Tirona’s departure was particularly consequential because he had held the presidency, chief operating officer position, and chief finance officer position at Lopez Holdings, all three of which were taken over by Piki’s brother Jay. The departures and changes in corporate roles occurred amid the bitter contest for control, although the companies have not established an official reason linking each departure to the feud. It would be wrong to assume that every executive or director left because of pressure to choose sides.

Still, the timing raises legitimate questions about how professional managers and directors navigate a conglomerate when its controlling shareholders are divided. Independent directors, in particular, are expected to exercise judgment on behalf of the company and its shareholders, rather than simply follow the wishes of the family that controls it. Their responsibilities become especially important when a company is considering major transactions involving competing family interests.

There are also investors outside the family. Among the more prominent is businessman and Batangas Representative Leandro Leviste, who acquired shares in ABS-CBN as a Mother’s Day gift for his mother, Senator Loren Legarda. His investment, like those of other minority shareholders, has been affected by changes in the media company’s capital structure. When ABS-CBN issues new shares, existing investors who do not acquire additional shares can see their percentage ownership shrink. The same principle applies whether the investor is a prominent politician’s son or an ordinary shareholder who bought a small number of shares through the stock market.

blocks.caption: Dividing the Lopez empire: Who decides what a family business is worth?

blocks.text: Lenders and institutional investors have their own interests. They may care about management continuity, financial stability, and whether contracts remain enforceable when control of a company changes. A family settlement may satisfy the relatives while leaving a company with insufficient capital, divided management, or shareholders who question whether their interests were properly considered.

This is why a family-controlled conglomerate cannot be treated simply as a collection of properties that relatives are free to divide among themselves. The family may control the votes, but the companies have obligations to other shareholders and stakeholders.

The experiences of other business families suggest that a workable settlement requires more than a willingness to stop fighting. Relatives need a credible way to value their interests, a means of financing any buyout, and clear arrangements governing who will control the businesses afterward. If they remain together, they need rules for making decisions and resolving disagreements. If they separate, they need agreements covering not only the division of assets but also debts, continuing obligations, and any business relationships that will remain between them.

For the Lopezes, the process is still unfolding. Piki has strengthened his position over the energy and industrial businesses, while Gabby’s branch has sold its Lopez Inc., stake and is positioned to acquire Rockwell if the proposed transaction is completed. ABS-CBN is raising capital to stabilize its finances. The family may be moving toward a clearer separation of business interests, but the companies still have obligations to their shareholders, employees, creditors, and business partners.

Lawyers, bankers, directors, and advisers can help value shares, prepare agreements, arrange financing, and secure approvals. They can help relatives settle who gets what, and under what conditions. What they cannot guarantee is that the businesses will prosper once the relatives have gone their separate ways. And they cannot shield controlling families from their legal and financial obligations to minority shareholders, creditors, and employees who never voted on the feud, yet have to live with its terms.

The Lopez cousins may eventually discover that running different businesses gives them the freedom they wanted. Or they may find that separating ownership and control comes with costs that become apparent only years later.
Other families have already taken that road. What happened to them after the agreements were signed, the lawsuits withdrawn, and the relatives stopped sharing the same boardroom? – Rappler.com
Part 3 on Friday, November 20 | Two cousins, two big bets: Will the Lopez split actually work?

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.

articles.title: Florida pastor found guilty over role in assassination of Haitian president
articles.summary: Christian Emmanuel Sanon is convicted of involvement in the plot that resulted in the killing of Jovenel Moïse.

blocks.text: A Florida pastor has been found guilty of a number of charges relating to the assassination of the Haitian President Jovenel Moïse.
Christian Emmanuel Sanon, a dual US-Haitian national, was convicted of all eight charges against him, including conspiracy to kill or kidnap a person. He faces a potential sentence of life in prison.

The 67-year-old was accused of being involved in a plot to replace Moïse as Haiti's president with himself in 2021, allegedly so he could award lucrative contracts to a Florida-based security outfit once in place.
The murder of Moïse has left Haiti without a leader for five years. That political vacuum has intensified gang violence in the impoverished Caribbean nation.
A presidential election is scheduled for next year and Moïse's wife, Martine, who was injured in the attack that killed her husband, announced this week that she intended to stand.

Sanon was found guilty on Wednesday following an eight-week trial in federal court in Miami, according to CBS, the BBC's US partner. His lawyer said he maintains his innocence and that he intends to appeal against the verdict, it reports.

Prosecutors said Sanon had "political aspirations" in Haiti and, in April 2021, met several other co-conspirators to devise a plan to oust Moïse in an armed raid on the presidential palace in the capital, Port-au-Prince.

Among them were the heads of the companies Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security - collectively referred to as CTU - who would finance the coup in exchange for government contracts for infrastructure projects, and to provide security forces and equipment.

A few months later, the other conspirators realised that Sanon had "neither the constitutional qualifications nor the popular support" to become Haiti's president and so shifted to another candidate, the US Department of Justice said.
At the same time, the plot had developed from one to forcibly remove Moïse from office to assassinating him, investigators said.
Dozens of people have been implicated in the conspiracy, which prosecutors said involved co-ordinating funding for and delivering weapons and mercenaries to Haiti to carry out the attack.

On 6 July that year, a group of Colombian mercenaries entered the presidential palace and killed Moïse. His wife, who was also injured in the attack, said at the time that the assailants had "riddled" her husband with bullets.
The successful assassination plot raised questions in Haiti about the relative ease with which the mercenaries were able to gain access to the president.

The country - the poorest in the Americas - has been ravaged by gang violence for years, but Moïse's assassination ushered in a period of worsening instability that emboldened gangs and prompted the deployment of a multinational force.
However, this has struggled to penetrate areas where gangs hold sway and more than 5,700 people have been killed or injured in the year to 11 September, the UN said last month.

Sanon and several other co-conspirators were arrested by Haitian authorities, while three mercenaries were killed in a gun battle with police. Eighteen people were transferred to Florida in September to stand trial over the plot.

Four men, including the heads of the CTU, were convicted of their role earlier this year. Sanon had been scheduled to be tried with them, but his case was delayed due to health reasons, according to CBS.
Sanon was born in Haiti but moved to the US as a teenager. He told the court he had worked in churches in Haitian immigrant communities in several parts of the US including Florida, US media report.

articles.title: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya, top UN court rules
articles.summary: The International Court of Justice has upheld large parts of a genocide case against Myanmar linked to the 2017 conflict with its Rohingya minority. It called for it to pay reparations and let…

image.caption: The ICJ's Yuji Iwasawa read out the ruling in The HagueImage: Piroschka van de Wouw/REUTERS

blocks.text: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday found Myanmar in breach of several of its obligations under international treaties to prevent and not to commit genocide.
The ICJ's president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa said that the panel of 15 judges had decided by nine votes to six that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya in Rakhine state.
The judges also found the country guilty of a series of other more specific violations by majority rulings.

"On the basis of all the evidence taken together, the Court is of the view that the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar's actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of... the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State," ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said.
Iwasawa said that Myanmar should make efforts to pay reparations to victims or their associates where possible and appropriate.
He also called for it to facilitate the safe return of refugees, and to take measures to investigate and if necessary prosecute individual wrongdoing by its nationals and security forces.

blocks.caption: Information on the Rohingya's legal battles is on show at the Cox' Bazar refugee camp in BangladeshImage: Md Zakir Hossain/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: What Judge Iwasawa said as he read out the verdict against Myanmar

The ICJ said that by its consideration, the Rohingya constituted a distinct ethnic group with their own defining language and culture, as well as self-identifying as such. This means they qualified as a protected group for the purposes of international laws against genocide.

Myanmar's security forces "killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated acts of sexual violence, as well as extreme violence against children," and also attacked Rohingya as they tried to flee the fighting, the ICJ's Iwasawa said.
"The court is fully convinced that the 2017 clearance operations caused serious bodily and mental harm to a significant number of the protected group," Judge Iwasawa said.

Iwasawa also said that some civilian participation in the clearance operations could not necessarily be considered state-ordered or state-sanctioned behavior. But the court found that the government and security forces also made no meaningful efforts to prevent non-Rohingya civilian atrocities and if anything fanned the flames of ethnic and religious tension.

blocks.caption: Ko Ko Hlaing represented Myanmar's government in the courtImage: Piroschka van de Wouw/REUTERS

blocks.text: At one point reading the details of the findings, Iwasawa noted "Myanmar's failure, genuinely to investigate the alleged atrocities, and its refusal to facilitate access to evidence and witnesses, or provide information requested."
He said this meant it was possible the court did not have reliable knowledge of information available only from within Myanmar to which it was not given access.
What is the genocide case against Myanmar?
The case centers around the military crackdown in Rakhine state on the country's western coastline against the predominantly Muslim Rohingya minority in 2017.

Violence had been brewing for several years beforehand, but the most intense phase of the military crackdown in the north of region was triggered by a coordinated attack by a Muslim militia group against several police and military installations and personnel in August 2017.

A UN fact finding mission later concluded that some 10,000 people likely died in the military clearance operations that followed. Around 700,000 people fled to Bangladesh, where most still reside in the world's largest refugee camp.
The Gambia filed the complaint at The Hague in 2019, alleging a deliberate campaign of arson, rape and murder designed to wipe out the Rohingya minority in whole or in part.

blocks.caption: The Gambia's Justice Minister and Attorney General Dawda Jallow attended the sessionImage: Piroschka van de Wouw/REUTERS

blocks.text: Myanmar's influential military, now back in full de facto control of the country albeit amid a long-running civil war, has maintained that it was engaged in a legitimate counterinsurgency.

Aung San Suu Kyi, who was the civilian president at the time, took a slightly more nuanced stance, but nevertheless traveled to The Hague to contest the charges, calling them "incomplete and incorrect."

The case is likely to draw close attention from those pursuing ICJ prosecutions against Israel and Benjamin Netanyahu for the war in Gaza and against Russia and Vladimir Putin for the invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title: Hakeem Jeffries on brink of Senate history as he tells Democrats to ‘fight Maga, not each other’ – US politics live
articles.summary:
Democrats resoundingly nominated Jeffries to serve as speaker of the House when the new Congress is sworn in next year

Denmark’s parliament on Thursday approved a hard-wrought…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 28m agoHakeem Jeffries on brink of Senate history as he tells Democrats to 'fight Maga extremism, not each other'

blocks.text: Denmark’s parliament on Thursday approved a hard-wrought agreement with Greenland and the United States to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.
The vote follows months of pressure by president Donald Trump seeking to control Greenland, a semiautonomous territory of Denmark, a Nato ally.

The trilateral deal - between Trump and the Danish and Greenlandic leaders – paves the way for more US bases in Greenland and eases tensions over Trump’s repeated calls for the vast island to become part of the US.

The 109-0 vote in the Folketing amounts to a final step, with the deal expected to enter into force once Denmark and Greenland has signed on. Greenland’s parliament approved the deal earlier this month, also with no opposition.
Hakeem Jeffries on brink of Senate history as he tells Democrats to 'fight Maga extremism, not each other'
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Hakeem Jeffries said it is the job of Democratic lawmakers to “fight Maga extremism” as he stood on the brink of becoming the first ever Black house speaker.
Democrats on Wednesday resoundingly nominated Jeffries to serve as speaker of the House when the new Congress is sworn in next year.

A New York congressman who has served as the Democratic minority leader since 2023, Jeffries is set to become one of Donald Trump’s most prominent opponents for the final two years of his presidency, when Democrats will control both the Senate and House of Representatives and are expected to undertake aggressive efforts to check his powers.

After his nomination was secured during closed-door voting, 251-11, ahead of a full House vote, Jeffries promised to take on the Trump administration’s Maga approach to governing the US. “Our job is to fight Maga extremism, not each other,” he said, “and to get big things done for the American people.”

Democrats nominated Jeffries despite concerns from some progressives that he represents a politically risky status quo for a party that is looking to capitalize on a surprisingly good performance in the midterms, where voters swept them back into power in the House and Senate with significant majorities.
He would become the first Democratic House speaker since Nancy Pelosi, who will retire from Congress at the end of this year.

Meanwhile today, president Trump has left China after hailing his trilateral meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, saying the three leaders were “really making history”. Trump said the US, Russia and China, the world’s largest nuclear powers, were “uniquely positioned” to discuss reducing their nuclear stockpiles.
You can follow the latest from Apec in our live blog here:
In other developments:

items: During a fiery House hearing, Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, defended his decision to take a government plane to attend a college football game, while thousands of flights had been cancelled and the airspace closed during the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) nationwide grounding over the weekend. “You want to bring up the fact that I took my family and my great nieces to an [Lousiana State University] game that was scheduled for weeks prior because I wanted to be a good uncle,” Mullin said, following questions from Congressman Bennie Thompson, the homeland security committee’s top Democrat.

Elon Musk called his midterm political spending “foolish.” After pouring nearly half a billion dollars into the election, in a Wednesday conversation with The New York Times’s DealBook Summit, Musk said: “If I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money.”

US Transportation secretary Sean Duffy blamed contractor L3Harris for last week’s nationwide ground stop. As legislators press for more answers on last week’s outage that caused thousands of flights to be halted, Duffy has continued finger-pointing, telling digital media outlet 2WAY on Wednesday that L3Harris, the aerospace and defense company whose router malfunctioned during an update, did not identify the issue “quick enough.”

Trump’s contentious triumphal arch continues to face setbacks. A federal judge extended the construction ban for the arch, slated for the Memorial Circle in Washington DC. A group of veterans and members of the Kennedy family members have blasted the project as disrespectful to those interred at the Arlington national cemetery.

articles.title: Mark Speakman resigns and says Liberals face ‘existential threat’ as NSW exodus continues
articles.summary:
Former NSW opposition leader warns party against becoming ‘Labor lite’ or ‘One Nation lite’ in late-night speech

  • Get our

blocks.text: Former New South Wales opposition leader, Mark Speakman, will not contest his seat at the March state election, the latest in a mass exodus of MPs under the Liberal leader who replaced him, Kellie Sloane.

In a late-night speech on Thursday, the final sitting day of NSW’s legislative assembly ahead of the vote, Speakman said he would not contest his south Sydney seat of Cronulla, which he has held since 2011.

He is the eighth out of 24 current Liberal MPs to announce they will not re-contest their seat in March, following Jordan Lane, Mark Coure, Tanya Davies, Ray Williams, James Griffin, Mark Taylor and Alister Henskens.
The announcement comes almost a year to the day after Speakman resigned from the leadership of the opposition in a spill in favour of Sloane, who was elected unopposed.
In that time the Coalition has gone from commanding 28% of the primary vote to 23%, Sydney Morning Herald Resolve polling suggests.
Labor has gone from 37% to 30%, while One Nation, which Resolve did not start polling separately until March, is currently at 26%.

Last week, Sloane said her party would not form government with One Nation, but she did not rule out a confidence and supply arrangement. The Australian Financial Review has reported many of her MPs privately expect the party to go into a coalition with the party.

In his speech in the dying minutes of the parliamentary term, Speakman, a member of the party’s moderate faction, warned the Liberals against becoming “Labor lite” or “One Nation lite”, saying they should stick to the values of “Menzian Liberalism”.
Referencing Pauline Hanson’s notion of “monoculture”, Speakman said Australia was “the most successful multicultural society on the planet” and was “so much better for it”.
“You know, we hear certain people say we want a monoculture, and that people who don’t support that monoculture somehow are enemies of Australia, hate Australia,” he said.
“I love Australia for its multiculturalism. Diversity is our strength. It is our strength, and we should build on that.”
Speakman, a barrister, served as minister for the environment between 2015 and 2017, and was attorney general between 2017 and the Perrottet government’s defeat in the 2023 election.
He was chosen as Liberal and opposition leader following Perrottet’s resignation, a position he held until November last year.

On Thursday, he said being opposition leader “is often said to be the toughest job in politics” and while it had “ultimately unravelled” for him, he had mostly led an opposition “which was competitive with, or even ahead of, the government in the polls”.

He said his record as attorney general included legislating for NSW to be the first Australian jurisdiction to criminalise coercive control, introducing affirmative consent tests in criminal sexual assault trials and reforming criminal and civil child sexual abuse cases.

Speakman’s resignation, ending speculation which bubbled up again when he spoke during question time on Thursday, is the latest blow for Sloane, who he said in his leaving speech had the “attributes to be a great premier”.
Earlier on Thursday, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, announced former Liberal councillor and parliamentary staffer Tanya Raffoul would contest the Liberal-held seat of Epping as a Labor candidate.
