articles.title: Elon Musk says record spending on US midterms was 'pretty foolish'
articles.summary: The multi-billionaire also said he was "not Maga", distancing himself from the political movement linked to Trump.

blocks.text: Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican defeats.
The Tesla and SpaceX CEO was the campaign's top individual donor, giving $446m (£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, particularly in Texas where many of Musk's firms are based.
Musk, who had backed Trump's second White House bid, also said he was "not Maga" - the Make America Great Again movement associated with the president.
Democrats won control of the Senate and House, while Texas, Ohio and other states swung away from Trump, who has faced pressure over the impact his policies have had on the cost of living.
Musk was speaking virtually at the New York Times DealBook Summit, an annual conference hosted in the city attended by major business and political leaders.
"I'm not Maga," Musk said, referring to the right-wing political movement.
He added: "I'm not sure what Maga means... if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that."
Musk went on to say he did not see much for the money he had spent on the Republicans' campaign, though he added that it was likely that candidates would have fared worse without the spending.
One of the most striking midterms wins went to Democrat James Talarico, who beat Republican Ken Paxton for a US Senate seat in Texas.
According to BBC analysis, Musk had spent at least $45m in support of Paxton.
Texas is where key operations for Musk's car company Tesla and rocket and technology firm SpaceX are based.
Democrats have vowed greater scrutiny of tech companies, including over the roll out of controversial data centres.

articles.title: Crimean Bridge attacked again, Russian official says
articles.summary: The head of Crimea said traffic was suspended after another attack on the link between Russia and the occupied territory.

blocks.text: Final moments before stretch of Crimean Bridge collapsed after Ukrainian attack
The Crimean Bridge has been attacked by Ukraine for the third time this week, a Russian official has said.
The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that traffic was temporarily suspended following another strike on the bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea.
The critical bridge had already been hit twice earlier in the week resulting in severe damage and part of the bridge collapsing into the water.
The important infrastructure has long been targeted by Ukraine because of its significance as a logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A screengrab of the damaged Crimean bridge in the Kerch Strait on 17 November

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
A screengrab of the damaged Crimean bridge in the Kerch Strait on 17 November
It comes as Russian President Vladimir Putin meets US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping on Thursday for landmark talks in China.
Aksyonov confirmed the strike on the bridge in the early hours of Thursday via Telegram, adding that assessment of the damage was under way.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian sources have continued to issue air raid alert warnings overnight for districts just outside of the capital Kyiv.

At least three people were killed in a Russian drone attack on Odesa on Wednesday, according to the regional state administration. Officials described the attack as "brutal and deliberate... directly targeting people and their lives".
President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge as an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Ukraine used drones and missiles against it on 17 November which brought down a key section of the road.
That section of the double-arched, 12-mile bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse.
In response, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".

While Ukrainian forces have struggled to close the bridge for good, recent attempts have brought them closer to destroying the bridge's crucial road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line.
Russian forces have also targeted key bridge crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv in recent days.
Russian strikes hit the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges causing traffic closures, partial damage to the metro system and some power and water outages.

articles.title: Van Gogh painting sells for record $190.4m after row over its Nazi history
articles.summary: Châtaigniers en fleurs was painted in 1890 in the final two months of Vincent van Gogh's life.

blocks.text: It was not immediately clear who purchased the painting. The BBC has contacted Sotheby's for comment.
The oil painting, which was estimated to carry a value of $180m (£136m) prior to the sale, was put up for auction as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.

Sotheby's announced in the hours before the auction that it had resolved a dispute between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the heirs of the Fischer family - the prior German owners of the work - regarding the sale.
Representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family had claimed the painting may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.

A lawyer for the family's heirs reportedly wrote to Sotheby's on their behalf, telling the auction house that the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis. The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.

"In recognition of the painting's complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement," Sotheby's said on Wednesday.
Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.
It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.
The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotheby's said.
Four other owners then had the painting.
The Blaquier family acquired it in 1975 and owned it for more than half a century before the latest sale, the auction house said.

articles.title: Russian man accused of spying on US tech defence company that assists Ukraine
articles.summary: The suspect followed employees and and was found with fake US ID documents and two Russian passports, US prosecutors say.

blocks.text: US investigators have arrested a Russian man who they say was recruited by Moscow to spy on employees of a technology and defence firm in California's Silicon Valley that has links to Ukraine.
Igor D'iu is accused of acting as an agent of a foreign government to conduct a spying operation in Palo Alto, near San Francisco.
He is also accused of stalking employees of the company and possessing falsified identity documents.

The company is not named in charging documents, but is described as a publicly traded technology and defence company that produces software used by Ukraine in its war with Russia. US prosecutors say the company was targeted by Russia due to its assistance to Kyiv.

"The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company's assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia," said US Attorney for the Northern District of California Craig Missakian.
"We will not tolerate any efforts - by foreign governments or otherwise - to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations."
Prosecutors say that D'iu entered the US unlawfully via the Mexico border, after travelling there from Istanbul in June.

He was allegedly recruited through the Telegram encrypted messaging app. His handlers referred to Russia as "'the Motherland' and directed D'iu to gather information about the company because it was supplying weapons used against Russia in Ukraine".
On their instruction, he purchased computers, phones, wireless networking equipment and remote access software - tools he needed for his spy mission.
He then went to a coffee shop located near the company's offices in Palo Alto, where he photographed laptop screens of employees who were working there.

His handlers also allegedly "instructed him to position his laptop at designated locations near the company so they could remotely access it and attempt to collect information from company employees in the vicinity".
According to CBS News, the BBC's US partner, the company in question is Palantir Technologies. Palantir did not reply to a BBC request for comment.
D'iu also allegedly conducted surveillance of employees and their residences.

On 3 September, he followed a vehicle driven by one senior executive for nearly 30 miles. He fled after she drove to a police station. Police later obtained evidence that he had followed other employees' cars on previous days.
During the investigation, officials discovered identity cards that had been falsified - including a US passport, California ID card, and a Social Security card with the fake name "Hugo Landry Johns".

A raid on his home in October in East Palo Alto turned up two Russian passports, and a handwritten notebook that contained numerous home addresses of employees "family members' names, educational and employment histories, and assessments of their strengths and weaknesses", prosecutors say.

He faces two charges related his alleged work as a foreign agent, one charge of interstate stalking, and one count of fraud related to his identity documents. He faces over 15 years in prison if found guilty.

articles.title: Israeli tanks cross ‘yellow line’ boundary into Hamas-controlled central Gaza
articles.summary:
First incursion across boundary since ceasefire deal comes as Eisenkot seeks to form government without Netanyahu

The Israeli military crossed into Hamas-controlled central Gaza on Wednesday…

blocks.text: The Israeli military crossed into Hamas-controlled central Gaza on Wednesday in its first ground operation across the “yellow line” boundary since a fragile ceasefire was agreed last October, forcing dozens of displaced Palestinians to flee their tents.

Israeli tanks rolled along the Salah al-Din road, Gaza’s main north-south route, a day after the US-backed Board of Peace, a body overseeing the ceasefire, accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities.
An Israeli military spokesperson said troops were carrying out an operation targeting “Hamas infrastructure” west of the yellow line in central Gaza.

The military ​has not commented extensively on the operation, which came as the Israeli opposition politician, Gadi Eisenkot, has been seeking to form a government without the caretaker prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who has built his political reputation on promises to keep Israel safe.

A Gaza security source told AFP there was “intense Israeli artillery shelling” north of Nuseirat refugee camp and reported Israeli military vehicles in central Gaza “amid ongoing gunfire and airstrikes since midday”.

Hamas condemned the Israeli raid and the forced displacement of Palestinians as “a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement” and a dangerous escalation. The Israeli military did not immediately respond to Hamas’s statement.
Residents reported hearing tank fire in the area. Palestinian medics said one person was killed in an Israeli airstrike near the site of the raid.

In separate incidents on Wednesday, Palestinian medics said two people were killed by Israeli fire, one in Deir al-Balah and the other in Gaza City. The Israeli military said it was unaware of any incident in Deir al-Balah and had struck a militant in Gaza City.
Israel has stepped up its attacks on Hamas, which it says has been regrouping and rearming. Hamas has accused Israel of trying to derail the US-brokered ceasefire agreed in October 2025.
Israeli strikes have continued since the ceasefire, and Hamas remains armed.
Last week, an Israeli airstrike on Nasser hospital in southern Gaza killed six people, including a surgeon and a disabled man, and wounded 28 others, according to the hospital director.

The body overseeing Donald Trump’s plan to end the war in Gaza has accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities, leaving Palestinians in dire conditions and the ceasefire at risk of collapse.

In its second report to the UN security council since the truce began 13 months ago, the Trump-led Board of Peace said the gap between what was agreed and what was happening on the ground remained the biggest threat to the deal. The report, seen by Reuters, warned that “a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely”.
Gaza’s health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire came into effect. The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.

Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in Gaza since Israel launched its military campaign in response to the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed.
Reuters and AFP contributed to this report

articles.title: Florida pastor found guilty over 2021 assassination of Haitian president
articles.summary:
Christian Emmanuel Sanon faces life in prison after conviction on charges arising from killing of Jovenel Moïse

A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted on…

blocks.text: A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted on Wednesday of US charges arising from the 2021 assassination of the Haitian president Jovenel Moïse.

Christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on charges including conspiring to kill Moïse after a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami. He had faced a total of eight charges including conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the United States.
He faces up to life in prison at sentencing.

Federal prosecutors said south Florida was a hub for planning and financing the plot to oust Moïse and install a president of the conspirators’ choosing. The government said Sanon was the conspirators’ initial choice for Moïse’s replacement. Prosecutors also said Sanon helped raise money for the conspiracy and arranged travel to Haiti and lodging for himself and others in that country.

Sanon acknowledged in trial testimony that he was in communication at one point with people trying to replace Moïse, but pointed out that the group had moved on to another candidate long before the assassination. He denied any knowledge of plans to kill Moïse.
Sanon was born in Haiti and moved to the US as a teenager. He testified that he worked with churches in Haitian immigrant communities in Florida and the midwest.

Haiti has not had a president since authorities said that a squad of mostly retired Colombian soldiers killed Moïse and wounded his wife in a night-time raid at their home on 7 July 2021. The poorest country in the Americas, Haiti has a history of dictatorship, political upheaval and foreign intervention that has long hindered democratic rule.
The election of a new president is scheduled for next year.

Prosecutors said the scheme to kill Moïse included paying about two dozen foreign mercenaries with money obtained from US government programs that were intended to help businesses during the Covid pandemic, according to court records. US prosecutors have charged more than 40 people with crimes related to the assassination and a dozen have been convicted, including five who are serving life sentences.

The plot to oust Moïse began taking final shape in April 2021, when Sanon met in south Florida with a former Haitian senator and several US businesspeople, according to an indictment. The group agreed that Sanon, once in power, would award contracts to two Florida-based companies – Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security, collectively known as CTU – for infrastructure projects, security forces and military equipment, according to investigators.

CTU initially hired about 18 Colombian nationals with military training to provide security for Sanon, according to prosecutors. Conspirators also spent months obtaining weapons and body armor and attempting to build ties with Haitian gangs, officials said.

By June 2021, the conspirators realized Sanon had neither the constitutional qualifications nor sufficient popular support to become president. They shifted their support to Wendelle Coq Thélot, a former Haitian supreme court judge who died in January 2025 while a fugitive.
Sanon was previously scheduled to be tried with four other men who were convicted earlier this year, but his case was separated from theirs and delayed for health reasons.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI is a love story. No to hiring sex workers, yes to buying your girlfriend flowers

image.caption: Jason and Lucia, the lead characters of Grand Theft Auto VI, can be played as a romantic couple or something more like platonic partners in crime. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Players jumping into Grand Theft Auto VI today may be surprised that they aren't able to commit some of the more morally objectionable acts that were possible in previous instalments.
Players can build lead couple's romantic relationship instead of hiring prostitutes
This story contains spoilers for the first chapter of Grand Theft Auto VI
The latest game in the series best known as crime and mayhem simulators doesn't let the main characters Jason or Lucia hire sex workers.
Earlier GTA games earned notoriety for letting players pay for a lap dance or sex, and then kill the sex workers and steal the money off their bodies.
Such indignities were possible, though never an objective or featured in the story.

Strippers still feature in GTA VI — both male and female, in a possible series first. An early mission has you talking to club patrons and throwing money at strippers as they dance, sometimes on poles. But you can't hire them for closer encounters.
The reason, Rockstar Games says, is simple: your leading duo are a couple.
Strippers still feature prominently in Grand Theft Auto VI, but the player cannot hire them for sex. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)
GTA VI "is a game about a couple in a bind, lovers on the run," the studio said in a statement to the tech site Shack News.

"Many aspects of previous titles are not present… but the elements we have we believe are all necessary and complementary to the feeling and motivations we wanted to emphasize as you play through Jason and Lucia's story."
PHOTOS | Gamers react to GTA VI:

That doesn't mean you're restricted from other kinds of mischief and high-level felonies, of course. Players can choose to play Jason and Lucia as more like platonic partners in crime, and the game still revolves around stealing cars, robbing businesses from corner stores to banks, and escaping the police.

You can still crash into other drivers along the road or even run over unnamed civilians in the city streets — though the consequences could be more severe than in past instalments, as witnesses (or survivors) might call the cops, pull a gun on you themselves, or chase you for kilometres and try to drive you off the road.
A user on Bluesky comments on an early mission in the game in which the player, as Jason, has to buy groceries for Lucia. (UltimaShadow/Bluesky)
As players around the world have gotten their hands on the game, however, some of their first reactions focused on the love story.
After some scene-setting flashbacks, the opening chapter starts with Jason, who's been working odd jobs for a drug dealer named Brian (voiced by Stephen Root).
As he learns that Lucia will soon be released from prison, the player can take time to repair his seaside home: patching up the roof, replacing rotted wooden stairs and painting the bedroom.
All of these actions build up Jason and Lucia's "relationship meter" — the higher the score, the more in sync the two will be throughout their adventures.
Players must manage Jason and Lucia's romantic relationship because how close they are may impact the story. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

Players will find several ways to build their romance; from Jason buying flowers for Lucia before their reunion, to spending more time playing both characters rather than just one. Button prompts make them hold hands while walking together, or simply hug and kiss with multiple animations of the two cuddling or giving a peck on the cheek.
It's a far cry from previous games' protagonists, including GTA V which included Michael, a middle-aged former gangster stuck in a loveless marriage and Trevor, an unhinged psychopath.
It's about family
Jason and Lucia's relationship comes into even greater focus in the early moments of the game.

In a moment of desperation, we see Lucia leave a restaurant to try to rob a nearby payday loans store. It goes poorly and as she's arrested, she shouts that she needs to go back to the restaurant. The camera then shows us a baby carrier with Lucia and Jason's infant son, Tomas.

items: GTA VI is a spectacular, cynical and sometimes shallow joyride
Skipping work to play Grand Theft Auto VI? You're not alone

blocks.text: As the couple reconnect after Lucia's release, they set an objective to make enough money (by doing crime, of course) to put into a family savings account for a future with their son.

That narrative focus flips the usual expectations of a Grand Theft Auto story, and might make a player less likely to engage in the seediest or most violent possible actions compared to in previous games, according to Kotaku writer Kenneth Shepard.

"In some ways, I can see the argument that Jason and Lucia could be willing to go to great lengths to reunite with their son and give him a comfortable life; I’m just not sure I see explosions and constant carnage on the path to that future now," he wrote Thursday, noting that he's only just started playing the game.
Lucia prepares for a robbery early in Grand Theft Auto VI. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jonathan Ore is a writer and editor for CBC Radio Digital in Toronto. He regularly covers the video games industry for CBC Radio programs across the country and has also covered arts & entertainment, technology and the games industry for CBC News. You can reach him at jonathan.ore@cbc.ca
